articles.title: This was the last lake of its kind in Canada. Now it's gone.
articles.summary: Canada's last epishelf lake — made up of freshwater floating on saltwater — is gone, along with the unique ecosystem it supported, scientists confirm. Here's what made the lake special, and what it…

image.caption: Jérémie Bonneau tries to free a probe called a mooring from the ice of the Milne Fiord epishelf lake in 2018. The lake was ice-covered year-round and was the last of its kind in Canada until it drained into the ocean in 2020. (Yulia Antropova/Water and Ice Research Laboratory/Carleton University)

blocks.text: Science·New

Canada's last epishelf lake — made up of freshwater floating on saltwater — is gone, along with the unique ecosystem it supported, scientists confirm. Here's what made the lake special, and what it disappearance says about the transformation of the Arctic in a warming climate.
In a polar epishelf lake, freshwater floats on seawater, creating a unique ecosystem
Canada's only remaining epishelf lake — made up of freshwater floating on saltwater — is gone, along with the unique ecosystem it supported, scientists confirmed in a new study.

Jérémie Bonneau, the lead author and an assistant professor at Laval University in Quebec City, said its loss is sad, as the Milne Fiord epishelf lake on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut was "the last thing like that in Canada."
"Suddenly, it's … drained away and then everything that was living in there is gone."
Bonneau noted that the complete disappearance of a once common phenomenon shows how a warming climate is transforming the Arctic.

While scientists had previously reported the lake's demise, the new study, recently published in the journal Scientific Reports, details how it happened and says the irreversible loss "marks a regime shift and the end of a 4000-year era."
Major ice shelf lake in Canada has disappeared
How epishelf lakes form
Glaciers are rivers of ice. Typically, they flow into the sea, and so does any meltwater on their surface. Normally, that freshwater is quickly mixed into the seawater by wind and waves.
But the mouth of Milne Fiord has been dammed for thousands of years by the Milne Ice Shelf — a huge, flat piece of ice sitting on the ocean and attached to the north shore of Ellsemere Island.

The dam stopped freshwater from flowing into the ocean, allowing it to accumulate on top of the saltwater of the Arctic Ocean. It formed a floating layer because freshwater is less dense than saltwater.

Meanwhile, a layer of ice about 50 to 100 centimetres thick covered the lake year-round, protecting the freshwater and saltwater layers from winds that could have mixed them together — and making the lake invisible from the surface.
Bonneau said there's evidence the lake in Milne Fiord had existed and been accumulating freshwater for more than 4,000 years.

When researchers first measured it in 1983, its freshwater layer was 18 metres deep, said Andrew Hamilton, a University of Alberta researcher who co-authored the new study. That's similar to the height of a six-storey building.

While some epishelf lakes sit completely on top of an ice shelf — that's what epishelf means — the Milne Fiord epishelf lake was actually connected to the ocean by an under-ice channel in the ice shelf, which has been thinning for about a century.
A unique ecosystem

By looking at the bacteria, viruses and phytoplankton in the two layers of the lake, researchers discovered practically no overlap between the freshwater and saltwater communities living just 20 centimetres apart.
Bonneau said, "It's really two unique ecosystems in the same water column, and you don't get that anywhere else."

Mary Thaler, who previously analyzed water from the lake for DNA but was not involved in the new study, said that while humans or fish could easily swim across the invisible border between the fresh and saltwater, for single-celled organisms, it's "an unbreakable barrier."

Analysis by Thaler and her colleagues at Laval University found bacteria and more complex eukaryotic microbes, whose cells are similar to those of plants and animals, as well as viruses. They included species that usually live in sediments on the bottom rather than in the water itself. Some of the microbes found in the lake had never previously been reported in the Arctic.

But the lake also had an influence beyond its own borders. Hamilton sent a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) into the channel in the ice shelf, where freshwater flowed out of the lake, mixed with saltwater along the way and carried nutrients to a lower depth than they would otherwise be found.
It recorded video footage of ghostly sea anemones, scallops and sea stars thriving in complete darkness below 10 metres of ice, fed by the nutrients draining from the epishelf lake.
"We were absolutely astounded to find a full, flourishing ecosystem existing within kind of this ice channel," he said.
How the lake – and its inhabitants – met their end
Then, in 2020, the Milne Ice Shelf broke into pieces off the coast of Ellesmere Island, and its wall no longer held the lake in.
Reverberations of the Milne Ice Shelf collapse
The new study looks at what happened to the ice and the lake itself before and after the collapse.
The researchers had probes called moorings that ran from the floor of the fiord to the surface, measuring salinity at different depths.
They showed that within two months of the ice shelf breaking up, the freshwater had drained and none was left in the fiord.
Thaler said freshwater organisms living there would have died more or less instantly when mixed with seawater.

While the freshwater lake was ice-covered year-round, the saltwater fiord is ice-free for part of the summer, allowing it to warm and be mixed by wind and waves — a typical marine environment suitable for organisms different from those supported by the former lake.
"And so you kind of start to see this huge change," Bonneau said.
While epishelf lakes are now completely gone from Canada, a few still exist in Greenland and Antarctica.

"Unfortunately," Hamilton said, "I think their days are numbered…. This kind of highlights that we are on a one-way trip for some of these really astounding ecosystems that make up the beauty of our planet."

articles.title: More people are seeking emergency care for gambling, a new study says — and it's mostly men and boys
articles.summary: New research published Wednesday in The American Journal of Preventive Medicine, found a nearly 100 per cent increase in emergency department visits, in just the past few years, following the rapid…

image.caption: Researchers say there's been an increase of almost a third in people visiting emergency departments in Ontario because of their struggles with gambling disorders since rules around online gambling were relaxed. (Alexander Kirch / Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide, as well as gambling, alcohol and drug addition.
Teddy Wojtowicz hasn't gambled in about three years, after his betting habit cost him his career and enough money to have bought a house, and left him with a criminal record.
He says his addiction escalated from spending $20-$40 on a night out, to wasting his paycheque every two weeks, to getting payday loans — and writing $22,000 in cheques to himself from his workplace.
"When you're gambling and you see that you keep losing and you know that you're losing, there's some part of you saying, 'Well, the next time I'm gonna win,'" Wojtowicz said.

The former accountant, who also had an alcohol addiction, admitted himself to a hospital in Dauphin, Man., in April 2023, after he began to think about suicide, and went through weeks of treatment to deal with his gambling. It was the second time he had sought help in the past decade.

items: Sharp rise in young men contacting Ontario gambling helpline, researchers find
The night started with a $25 online sports bet. It ended in a $14K loss

blocks.text: Wojtowich is one of a rising number of men and boys who are turning to hospital emergency departments after reaching rock bottom with gambling and related addictions and disorders, according to a new study published Wednesday in The American Journal of Preventive Medicine.

Researchers in Ontario found a dramatic increase in emergency department visits in just the past few years, following the rapid growth of online gambling in that province and the legalization of betting on single sports events.
But those are just the people with acute harms related to gambling addiction, says Ryan Forrest, a public health doctoral student at the University of Toronto who co-authored the study.
"Anybody who gambles can experience harms," she told CBC News, saying these findings may not account for a much larger number of people who haven't reached the point of seeking support.
He helped legalize online gambling — now he wants to rein it in
Over 80 private gambling sites in Ontario

Forrest and co-author Dr. Daniel Myran logged 757 individuals who made a total of 952 emergency department visits in Ontario related to care for gambling disorders during a 14-year period beginning in 2012 — the year the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) rolled out online gambling.
The numbers marked a 31.3 per cent increase from before this time, when the number of visits was stable, the researchers said.
Although Ontario wasn't the first province introduce online gambling, it later led the way when it came to permitting private companies to operate in its market, in April 2022.
There are now more than 80 gaming and betting sites operated by over 40 private companies in the province.
Beyond that, Canada legalized single-game sports betting in 2021.
LISTEN | How online sports betting changed the game for everyone:
The Current23:54When it comes to sports betting, does everyone lose?
Forrest and Myran's research also suggests men and boys have been significantly affected, as they comprise 72 per cent of the total hospital visits.
Broken down by age and gender, hospital visits increased 154 per cent among males aged 10-29 and 116 per cent for men aged 30-44, compared to the years prior to the liberalization of gambling laws.
There was no notable increase among females.

Most of the people who went to an emergency department due to their gambling addiction often had associated substance use or mental health disorder, including thoughts of suicide, says Myran, a physician and associate professor with the department of family and community medicine at the University of Toronto.

"These are the very severe moments when people where people are showing up in crisis and gambling has either been the cause of that, mixed with other substance use, or it's been a contributing factor," he said.

Forrest says she hopes this data, and other research, will encourage other provinces and territories to consider that "liberalizing gambling in the way that has happened in Ontario is not good for people's health and well-being."
Sports betting ads put youth at risk of gambling addiction, doctors warn
Helpline study showed spike in demand
Other studies have sounded the alarm about the impact of online gambling and sports betting.

Research published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) in March found there was a 95.5 per cent increase in men and boys making gambling-related calls to ConnexOntario — the province's 24-hour mental health and addictions helpline — between the 2015 launch of the OLG's regulated online gaming portal PlayOLG and September 2025.
Among males aged 15-24 the increase was 317 per cent, according to the CMAJ study, which Forrest was also a part of.
LISTEN | Former MuchMusic, host Rick Campanelli on his recovery from gambling addiction:
53:59Rick Campanelli

Ottawa pediatrician Dr. Shawn Kelly, who specializes in adolescent addiction medicine, says the data has long been clear that gambling disorder is "considerably more common in males than females sort of across the ages."
The evidence should signal there needs to be an increased awareness and support for those struggling with gambling addiction, particularly younger males, he says.

items: Sharp rise in young men contacting Ontario gambling helpline, researchers find
More than a third of B.C. youth turning to gambling, gaming with money: report

blocks.text: He adds he has not seen any increase in suicidal thoughts or ideation related to gambling problems among the adolescents he's dealt with — "but we also see that there are worsening of anxiety disorder, worsening of school attendance problems there, worsening of depressive symptoms."
Adding to that, he says, is the significant financial harm it can cause families.

Kelly, who is not affiliated with either study, says access to smartphones and other devices at young ages means parents may need to watch for signs their child may be struggling with an online gambling habit.
Those signs could include preoccupations with money and sports scores, as well as withdrawal from family, school, work and other activities.
Sexy Sydney Sweeney ad triggers angry backlash — again
Hard to watch

Myran says the access and promotion of gambling treatment pales in comparison to the prevalence of new forms of gambling and the promotion of apps and betting services on television and social media — much of it targeting men.
For a recovering gambling addict like Wojtowich, it can be difficult just to watch sports because viewers are bombarded by ads.

Even though he has gone through treatment and is now working in peer support to help others overcome their addictions, he says it's hard to tune out hosts talking about odds and commercials for betting apps.
"It's troublesome to see," he said.
Wojtowich would like to see limits on gambling ads appearing on television, similar to restrictions on cigarettes.
Kelly agrees there needs to be more controls on the promotion of gambling.
"It's past time for us to detangle these things, so that watching a sports broadcast doesn't mean that we are being subjected to the powerful effects of this advertising," he said.
Controversial prediction market betting coming to Canada
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

articles.title: Cop wounded in gun attack at checkpoint in SGA-BARMM
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY- A police officer was wounded after unidentified armed men fired at a security checkpoint in Barangay Kadingilan, Nabalawag, Special Geographic Area (SGA), Bangsamoro Autonomous Region…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY- A police officer was wounded after unidentified armed men fired at a security checkpoint in Barangay Kadingilan, Nabalawag, Special Geographic Area (SGA), Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) on Wednesday, a police official said.
Capt. Steffi Salanguit, spokesperson for Police Regional Office Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PROBAR), identified the wounded officer as Pat. Alfadz Umal of the Regional Mobile Force Battalion 14-A.

The 33rd Infantry Battalion (33IB) reported the tension early Wednesday in Barangay Olandang, Nabalawag, following an exchange of gunfire involving armed individuals reportedly linked to the 118th Base Command and members of the 105th Base Command, both of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
The 33IB also immediately deployed troops to intervene and maintain peace and order.

Lt. Col. Germen Legada, 33IB commander, coordinated with the MILF’s Coordinating Committee on the Cessation of Hostilities (CCCH) members Ansari Manan and Abusaima to call for an immediate halt to the armed confrontation.

Salanguit said police established a checkpoint in front of the Kadingilan Barangay Hall as part of blocking and security operations, to assist motorists and evacuees and increase police visibility in the area.
At around 11:56 a.m., while police personnel were manning the checkpoint, they reportedly heard successive gunshots from an undetermined caliber of high-powered firearms.
Umal was hit in the right thigh.
Police personnel returned fire toward the suspected source of the gunfire before withdrawing to the municipal police station after the shooting temporarily subsided.
Umal was brought to a hospital in Midsayap, North Cotabato for medical treatment.
Security and checkpoint operations remain ongoing, while authorities continue to investigate the incident.
At least 800 families fled their homes for fear of getting caught in the crossfire, Kadingilan Punong Barangay Saiden A. Alim said./coa

articles.title: At least 12 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
articles.summary: Dozens of people are missing beneath the rubble of the building in Gaza City, where 10 families had reportedly been living.

blocks.text: At least 12 people have been killed, including children, and dozens are missing after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip, according to local rescue teams.
Video footage shows the search for bodies and survivors continuing in the rubble of the multi-storey building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, its floors sandwiched together.
Locals said 10 families had been living in the apartments despite warnings that they were unsafe.

Members of the Hamas-run Civil Defence rescue service said they had initially been working with "empty hands" due to tight Israeli restrictions on equipment allowed into Gaza. However, they have since been able to borrow some heavy machinery.
On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.
The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.
Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza.

articles.title: [OPINION] The HIV epidemic we saw coming — and can still stop
articles.summary: The Philippines' surging HIV epidemic stems from health-system execution failures, not individual behavior. To reverse it, the DOH must urgently expand testing, treatment, and incentives.

blocks.text: Not long ago, I was having dinner with a former health secretary from an earlier Philippine administration.

Our conversation turned to the extraordinary rise of HIV. I asked when the epidemic really began to accelerate, and why the Philippines had diverged so sharply from neighbors such as Thailand and Vietnam.
The answer surprised me. The instinctive explanation was essentially that young people today were having too much unprotected sex.
That is partly true. But it does not explain the Philippine anomaly.
Young people have sex in Thailand and Vietnam. HIV stigma and inconsistent condom use are hardly uniquely Filipino.
Yet estimated new HIV infections in the Philippines increased from around 4,400 in 2010 to 29,600 in 2024 — a 550% increase. Around 252,800 Filipinos were estimated to be living with HIV in 2025.
Vietnam moved in the opposite direction: new infections fell nearly 60%, from around 14,000 in 2010 to fewer than 6,300 in 2024. Thailand has reduced new infections by about 66% since 2010.
So the question is not simply why individuals acquire HIV. It is why the Philippine epidemic diverged so dramatically from those of comparable neighbors.
We saw it coming.
The critical Philippine period was arguably 2010 to 2014.
In 2010, the HIV registry recorded 1,591 newly diagnosed cases. That became 2,349 in 2011, 3,338 in 2012 and 4,814 in 2013. Annual diagnoses more than tripled in only three years.

And this was not simply more testing uncovering a stable epidemic. Among men who have sex with men, HIV prevalence in sentinel sites rose from 0.30% in 2007 to 1.05% in 2009, 2.12% in 2011 and 3.50% in 2013.
By 2011, prevalence was already reported at around 6% among MSM in Quezon City and 5% in Cebu, even while national prevalence remained very low.
Government therefore had a clear warning. But it still faced a much smaller and more concentrated epidemic than it does today.
UNAIDS estimated around 36,000 Filipinos were living with HIV in 2014, compared with roughly a quarter-million today.

Yet in 2013, the UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for AIDS warned that the country was spending only about US$8–10 million annually on HIV prevention, against an estimated requirement of at least US$40 million.
By 2014, only around 24% of people living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral therapy.
That is why this period matters. The epidemic was unmistakably accelerating, but before the reservoir of infection had reached today’s scale.
The missed opportunity was not one person’s failure. It was a health-system failure to translate surveillance into sufficiently aggressive execution.
In 2025 in Bangkok, I had the opportunity to meet Khun Mechai Viravaidya, Thailand’s famous “Mr. Condom.”
Thailand faced its own critical period decades earlier. Its response was strikingly different.

When HIV exploded there around 1990, the government did not simply tell people to behave better. It elevated HIV to a national priority. Prevention messages saturated radio and television. Condoms were aggressively distributed. The 100% Condom Programme targeted the transmission networks surveillance had identified. Mechai became one of the most visible faces of that response.

Within three years, condom use among sex workers reportedly increased from below 25% to more than 90%. HIV-prevention spending rose almost twentyfold to US$44 million by 1993. Estimated annual new infections subsequently fell from about 143,000 in 1991 to fewer than 14,000 in 2001.
Thailand did not eliminate risky behavior. It changed the environment in which transmission occurred. That distinction matters.

As HIV prevalence rises inside a sexual network, an individual does not necessarily need to become more sexually active for risk to increase. More infected partners are simply circulating within that network.
Meanwhile, undiagnosed and untreated infection allows transmission to continue.
The cycle becomes: undiagnosed infection → transmission → higher prevalence → greater exposure → more infections.

Treatment breaks that cycle. A person who achieves sustained viral suppression does not sexually transmit HIV. That is why simply blaming young people for unprotected sex is an inadequate public-health explanation.

Even today, Thailand is making progress in eliminating HIV. Dr. Nittaya Phanuphak, a pioneer of community-led PrEP and transgender health services, was named a 2026 WHO South-East Asia Public Health Champion — a recognition well deserved.

The Philippines has previously set a national goal of reaching 150,000 people with PrEP by the end of 2026. Yet only 55,284 had ever initiated PrEP by the end of 2024 — against an estimated MSM population alone of roughly 1.38 million.
Secretary Edwin Mercado merely inherited the epidemic. But he can become the health secretary under whom Philippine HIV incidence finally peaks and begins to fall.
That should be the metric: Did fewer Filipinos acquire HIV this year than last year? What is the PrEP target?
DOH should aggressively expand testing, immediate treatment, viral suppression and PrEP.
It should also question the assumption that making HIV testing free is enough.
Testing still carries costs: transportation, lost work time, inconvenience, stigma and fear.
There is already evidence that incentives can increase testing uptake.

In a randomized US emergency-department trial involving more than 8,700 patients, offering US$5 increased HIV-test acceptance by about 10 percentage points, while US$10 increased it by about 15 points compared with no financial incentive.

In Kenya, a randomized study found that offering US$5 or US$10 to caregivers to bring children of unknown HIV status for testing increased testing from 34% without an incentive to 55% and 61%, respectively.
The Philippines should test the same principle rather than debate it abstractly.
Offer modest incentives — perhaps transport credits, mobile load, pharmacy or food vouchers — to selected populations with low screening uptake.
Then measure the results.
The Philippines had surveillance. It had plans. It had the warning. The failure was translating warning into execution quickly enough.
Thailand’s experience offers a simple lesson:
When an epidemic moves quickly, public health must move faster.
Mercado’s DOH cannot change what happened in 2010. But it can determine what the Philippine HIV graph looks like in 2030.
Make this the period when HIV incidence finally peaks — and begins to fall. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

articles.title: Panganiban: Counting absent senators in voting threshold unfair
articles.summary: Former Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday said allowing senator-judges who did not participate in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte to vote and be included…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published September 16, 2026 3:53pm

Former Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban on Wednesday said allowing senator-judges who did not participate in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte to vote and be included in determining the threshold for conviction would be unfair, if not unjust, to the Filipino people.
“Fairness [in judgment] can be rendered by two-thirds of those present [Senators],” Panganiban said during questioning by Senator-judge Panfilo Lacson on Day 26 of Duterte's impeachment trial.

The amici curiae, or friends of the court, were asked to weigh in on the voting threshold for conviction, given that at least four incumbent senators have not been able to participate in the impeachment trial.
“They were not in a position to know the truth [by being absent]. How can they render fairness to our people? Those (truth and fairness) are the standards, simple standards," Panganiban said.

"I'm not going to ask you to follow the rules of court. I'm not going to ask you to follow the technicalities of the law. All I'm saying is, are you in a position to know the truth? Are you in a position to render a fair judgment? I think that should be the test,” he added.

He was responding to a question from Senator-judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on whether the Senate impeachment court could render a fair judgment if absent senator-judges were allowed to vote and were included in determining the threshold for conviction.
“If they're not in a position to know the truth, then they should not dare vote and participate because that will be unfair to our people,” Panganiban added.
Azcuna warns of possible SC challenge

Retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna, for his part, said using fewer than 16 votes as the threshold for conviction could expose the Senate impeachment court's ruling to a Supreme Court challenge because the Constitution requires a two-thirds vote of all members of the Senate for conviction.
“There could be grounds for Supreme Court intervention if a senator is not included in determining the threshold. The judgment could have a defect,” Azcuna said.
Azcuna warned that a conviction based on two-thirds of the participating senators, rather than two-thirds of all Senate members, could be challenged before the Supreme Court as unconstitutional.

“Supposing there is a judgment of conviction based on 23 instead of 24. Two-thirds of 23. That's 15... 15 votes to convict. And the Senate said convicted. That conviction ruling based on 15 votes could be reversed by the Supreme Court because it is violation of the Constitution because it is not two-thirds of all the members,” Azcuna said.
“That is just my take,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: English village votes to leave UK in protest over migrant housing plan
articles.summary:
Villagers in Piddington, Oxfordshire, hold symbolic referendum over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby

Residents of an English village have voted to leave the UK in a…

blocks.text: Residents of an English village have voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum against plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby.

The result of the poll in Piddington, Oxfordshire, was announced on Wednesday morning after 312 people voted on Tuesday. A total of 285 people were in favour of independence from the UK while 26 voted against. One ballot was spoiled.

The poll was organised by campaigners for residents to demonstrate opposition to government plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a converted Ministry of Defence site in the town of Bicester.

Reacting to the news, a government minister said she would “gently” tell residents of the village that the government was working to bring down the asylum backlog, and that a burden had to be shared across communities.

Lisa Nandy, the culture and media minister, told Sky News: “We are getting that backlog down. We’re speeding up the processing of claims, and in the meantime, we don’t think it’s acceptable for all of the burden of shouldering not just asylum accommodation, but also many other forms of temporary accommodation, to fall on poorer communities.”

She added: “That’s what we saw under the previous government. Because accommodation is cheap in many, not just towns, but in particular postcode areas. People who live in more deprived communities have had to put up with almost … every other house in some instances … turned into HMOs [house in multiple occupation], and that is not OK.”

The dispute over the plans in Bicester come against a backdrop of tensions elsewhere over the location of accommodation for asylum seekers. After disturbances in Thetford, Norfolk, earlier this year, which far-right activists attempted to exploit, the local Labour MP there voiced his concerns that cheaper, working-class areas were being chosen as locations for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.

blocks.caption: A ‘Principality of Piddington’ sign is placed on the village boundary. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: Tim Bearder, the leader of Oxfordshire county council, said on Wednesday that the result in Piddington showed that campaigners had done “an incredible job” to highlight their concerns.

“This referendum shows how strongly they feel about the proposal and that is partly about the proposal itself and partly about way the government has gone about it, without engaging with local people and looking at the feasibility of the site,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
“It’s the wrong site for the local community and for the asylum seekers themselves,” said Bearder, who declined to say what alternative sites could be used.
The result was announced on Wednesday morning by a “returning officer” in front of an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall.
A parish councillor, Mike Nixon, said the proposed site had no pedestrian access areas, and that the nearest path was about a mile and a quarter away, down a busy unlit road.

The Home Office has previously said that the government is closing asylum hotels in what is expected to saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support and that it is working fairly to house asylum seekers across the country.
“As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area,” a spokesperson said.

articles.title: ILO, Canada launch initiative in PH vs forced labor
articles.summary: The International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Canadian government have launched a four-year project aimed at strengthening responsive institutions and mechanisms to eliminate forced labor in…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 3:52pm

The International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Canadian government have launched a four-year project aimed at strengthening responsive institutions and mechanisms to eliminate forced labor in the Philippines.

PRIME PH is an initiative that will work with the Philippine government, labor and employer groups, and other stakeholders to strengthen policies and institutions, prevent and address forced labor, protect workers, and improve access to justice and remedies.
Supported by the Labour Program of Employment and Social Development Canada, it will run from 2026 until February 2030.
The ILO said eliminating all forms of forced or compulsory labor is a fundamental principle and right at work, essential to decent work, social justice, and human dignity.

“Forced labor has no place in our societies. Eliminating this practice is fundamental to achieving decent work, social justice, and human dignity,” said Khalid Hassan, Director of the ILO Country Office for the Philippines.

The initiative further aims to strengthen the Philippines’ compliance with international labor standards, promote decent work, and encourage responsible business practices, particularly in the manufacturing and agriculture sectors exporting to Canada.

“Protection from forced labor is fundamental to decent work, human dignity, and fair competition. The Philippines stands at the forefront of this effort, with strong labor standards that protect workers, uphold human rights, and strengthen our place in global trade,” said Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino.
According to the ILO, the risk of forced labor in the Philippines is particularly high in sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, and mining, as the practice is often hidden.
This makes it difficult to determine its true scale and identify workers who need protection.
However, forced labor has growing implications for the country’s trade and businesses.
The Canadian government defined forced labor as a “serious violation of human rights that demands a targeted response."

“The PRIME PH project will advance efforts in Philippine tradeable sectors to prevent forced labour and strengthen protections for workers. Through these types of partnerships, we can help build fairer workplaces while ensuring worker’s rights are respected.” said John Zerucelli, Canada’s Secretary of State for Labour.

“By working together, Canada and the Philippines can strengthen opportunities for workers and businesses alike by keeping workers’ rights at the heart of our economic partnership and creating lasting benefits for communities in both countries,” said Patty Hajdu, Canada’s Minister of Jobs and Families and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Northern Ontario.

PRIME PH was established to address labor gaps, prevent exploitation, protect victims of forced labor, strengthen enforcement, and promote responsible business practices through stronger cooperation among government, workers, employers, civil society, and other partners.

Nearly 100 representatives from government, workers’ and employers’ groups, civil society, development partners, academia, and the private sector joined the launch and reaffirmed their commitment to promoting decent work and ending forced labor. —RF, GMA News

blocks.caption: (From left to right): Marro Ventura, National Sales Manager; Francis Avila, Head of Commercial; Rico Hizon, ASUS  Business PH Brand Ambassador, Veteran Broadcast Journalist & Business Consultant; Jolla Valencia, Channel and  Territory Account Sales (Visayas); and Liang Chen, Country Product Manag…

blocks.text: Following its Manila debut on July 1, 2026, the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra made its regional debut in NUSTAR Resort Cebu, Cebu City on September 7 and 8, followed by Dusit D2, Davao City on September 11.

Drawing more than 1,000 total attendees, the Grand Launches supports ASUS Business Philippines’ commitment to expanding access to enterprise-grade AI for business technology. For ASUS Business, the message is clear: the next wave of AI adoption and business-grade devices are not limited to one place. It is also taking shape in the regional business hubs where companies are building, scaling, and competing for the future.

blocks.caption: Francis Avila, ASUS Business Philippines’ Head of Commercial

blocks.text: Bringing Business-Grade Technology Closer to Fast-Growing Regional Businesses

ASUS brought its flagship business laptop, the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra, to Cebu and Davao as part of its continued regional expansion and commitment to making its latest business grade devices more accessible in key regional markets.

As businesses in Visayas and Mindanao continue to expand, the demand for reliable, high performance technology that can support increasingly sophisticated workplaces is also growing. Bringing business-grade devices like ASUS ExpertBook Ultra closer to these markets allows regional businesses to experience the products firsthand, and explore solutions suited to their needs.

The tour kicked off in Cebu City on September 7 and 8, where more than 600 attendees filled the NUSTAR Resort Cebu. The Cebu launch was hosted by veteran broadcast journalist and ASUS Business Brand Ambassador Rico Hizon alongside co-host Andi Pateña-Mateu, featuring a special performance by Jacky Chang.

blocks.caption: (From left to right): Marro Ventura, National Sales Manager; Francis Avila, Head of Commercial; Neilbert Tan, Channel and  Territory Account Sales (Mindanao); and Liang Chen, Country Product Manager of Commercial Notebook

blocks.text: The tour continued in Davao on September 11, bringing more than 500 attendees together at Dusit D2 for the regional close. The event was hosted by Claire Lara, with a special performance by Aila Santos.

Both launches opened with an Expert Class Forum featuring sales training, a product showcase, and an exclusive first look at the ASUS Business product roadmap and upcoming programs. The event was followed by the Grand Launch, where guests witnessed live durability demonstrations, local dance performances, and a Gala Night that brought together business leaders for an evening of networking and celebration.

blocks.caption: ASUS ExpertBook Ultra Cebu Davao

blocks.text: Together, the Cebu and Davao launches mark an important step in ASUS Business Philippines’ regional expansion, bringing business-grade devices and support closer to the companies and professionals shaping the future of Visayas and Mindanao.
ASUS Business Brand Ambassador Rico Hizon leads the Cebu Launch as Host

blocks.caption: (from left to right) Rico Hizon, ASUS Business Philippines Brand Ambassador and Andi Pateña-Mateu, Co-Host of the  ASUS ExpertBook Ultra Grand Launch in Cebu

blocks.text: The Cebu Grand Launch also marked a significant moment for ASUS Business Philippines Brand Ambassador Rico Hizon, who took on the role of host for the launch.
As a veteran broadcast journalist and business consultant, Hizon brings 38 years of experience covering some of the world’s most consequential business stories.

The launch also featured a special “Murphy’s Law” video featuring ASUS Business ambassadors Gabbi Garcia and Rico Hizon for memorable demonstration of the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra’s durability and resilience. Together, they took on “Murphy’s Law”—the idea that anything that can go wrong, will go wrong—putting the flagship business laptop through a series of unexpected challenges and proving that even when things go wrong, the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra is built to keep going.
Watch the Video: Rico Hizon and Gabbi Garcia Beats Murphy’s Law with ASUS ExpertBook Ultra

Hizon represents the kind of modern business leader the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra is built to support: veteran executives who are constantly connected and navigating a professional landscape where portable devices, durability, business-grade security is becoming an increasingly important part of everyday work.
The Flagship AI PC Built for Modern Business

Boldy positioned as “The Flagship of the Industry. Period.” the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra weighs as little as 0.99kg and measures just 10.9mm thin. It combines an ultra-portable form factor with up to an Intel® Core™ Ultra X9 Series 3 processor, a dedicated NPU delivering 50 TOPS and up to 180 total platform TOPS.

As a certified Copilot+ PC, the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra also features built-in AI features such as ASUS MyExpert. With Military-Grade durability and up to 26 hours of battery life, it’s designed to withstand the demands of frequent business travel and support executives professionals who are constantly on the move.
No Price Increase: ASUS ExpertBook Ultra Retains Its ₱129,995 Introductory Price
Despite widespread price increases across the PC market, the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra maintains its introductory price of ₱129,995.

The decision reinforces ASUS’ aim to make its latest business technology more accessible to Philippine enterprises, SMBs, and professionals, particularly as businesses increasingly look to AI-powered business-grade devices to improve productivity and stay competitive.

articles.title: Foreign students to face tough restrictions on bringing in family under Labor’s immigration plan
articles.summary: Home affairs minister Tony Burke will detail long-awaited changes as support for One Nation surges amid immigration debate

blocks.text: Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia, as the federal government shifts sections of the country’s immigration system away from demand-driven settings.

Long-awaited changes will be revealed by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, on Thursday, and are expected to include efforts to stop visa overstays and limit lengthy appeals processes for applicants.
The changes are designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy.
Burke will address the National Press Club in Canberra, with a speech titled “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”.
He had been due to announce the plans more than a month ago, but the speech was cancelled at the 11th hour amid debate inside cabinet about the direction and scale of the changes.
The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, allowing the government more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country.
Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers, but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament.
“We do need to get net overseas migration down,” Burke said.
“We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy.”
Labor wants policy settings tweaked to ensure it can meet forecasts for Nom, as support for One Nation surges over concerns about rates of immigration.

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. Under the mooted changes, the vast majority of students would be required to come alone.

As well as 185,000 permanent arrivals annually, the government wants Nom to fall from about 305,000 to about 225,000 over two years, ending years of higher than expected arrivals, including from international students and working holidaymakers.

Nom measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months, including leaving and returning Australian citizens. Nom has fallen in seven consecutive quarters since September 2023. It is forecast to fall lower than pre-Covid levels by 2027-28.
But temporary visa holder rates remain high. For the 2024-25 financial year, there were 568,370 overseas arrivals, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.
Changes including efforts to stop people whose visas have expired from transferring to different categories are likely, essentially forcing some overseas citizens to leave the country more quickly.
The government is also expected to seek to drive down the number of unlawful non-citizens currently in Australia.
after newsletter promotion

Department of Home Affairs data shows that, as of July, there were 110,898 individuals not granted a protection visa who were yet to be deported. The total includes people on bridging visas and others seeking a judicial or administration review.
Labor’s efforts to regain the initiative on immigration comes as One Nation surges in the polls and as community sentiment on the number of overseas arrivals remains a key issue motivating voters.
One Nation said on Monday it would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.
Business groups, universities, the aged care sector and both Labor and the Coalition all savaged the plan, warning Hanson’s proposals would hurt essential services and the economy.

Anthony Albanese tried to secure Coalition support for legislative changes in talks with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, last week, but no agreement was reached. The prime minister leaves Australia to attend the United Nations general assembly in New York on Friday.
The independent senator David Pocock said on Wednesday the country deserved a mature conversation about immigration, not one starting with numbers.

“The big thing I would love to see is a plan. There’s this constant talk about numbers, about classes of visas. Rather than actually having the conversation as a country, what is our 10-year plan for migration,” he told ABC radio.
“What are the skills that we need? What are the trade-offs when it comes to housing, impact on the environment?”
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss, Andrew McKellar, called for an end to “the race for the lowest Nom”, warning business needed skilled workers from overseas.

“We do not have a migration problem in Australia; we have a housing crisis and skill shortages. Those are the problems we need to fix. Shortsighted approaches that damage the economy won’t solve them. Those are red lines for business,” he said.

articles.title: Kosovo ex-president Thaci faces Hague war crimes verdict
articles.summary: A tribunal will rule if Hashim Thaci, a former commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), committed war crimes during the war of independence with Serbia.

image.caption: Hashim Thaci has said he expects to be aquittedImage: Jerry Lampen/Reuters

blocks.text: A Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday will hand down its ruling in a three-year trial of former President Hashim Thaci and several commanders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) for war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed during the 1998-1999 independence war with Serbia.

Thaci, a former KLA political leader, and former high-ranking KLA guerrillas Jakup Krasniqi, Rexhep Selimi and Kadri Veseli, have all pleaded not guilty to multiple counts including murder, torture and persecution.
Prosecutors have requested 45-year prison sentences for each defendant.
What are the defendants accused of?
Prosecutors have said KLA forces killed more than 100 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces during and just after the Kosovo war.
This included prisoners held at KLA facilities in Kosovo and Albania, along with politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.
The defense has argued that the senior KLA figures could not control or be held responsible for such acts, as the group lacked a strict command structure.
Lawyers have argued there is no direct evidence linking Thaci's command to any of the alleged crimes.
"I expect to be acquitted of every charge," Thaci said in August.
Seen as heroes in Kosovo

The accused are revered as national heroes inKosovo, and the KLA and Thaci are seen as symbols of the independence movement. Thaci remained a central political figure after the war and was instrumental in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia.

The verdict in The Hague is being livestreamed in the Kosovo capital, Pristina, where thousands of Thaci and KLA supporters are expected to gather. This follows rallies over the weekend that drew tens of thousands calling for the men's acquittal. A huge digital clock is counting down to the verdicts on Wednesday.

blocks.caption: KLA supporters rallied in Pristina over the weekendImage: Zana Cimili/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Our war was just, a war of liberation," Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.
"We believe and hope … that the KLA leaders will return free to their country and to their families," he added.
After being indicted in 2020,Thaci resigned as president and has been detained in The Hague since then.
Tribunal deeply unpopular in Kosovo
Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors have tried to distinguish between Kosovo's struggle for independence from Serbia and the alleged crimes committed by the men on trial.

The tribunal responsible for prosecuting the case, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), was set up in 2016 after earlier cases in Kosovo failed due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.
Explainer: What are the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
Although based in The Hague, and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged KLA war crimes.
Nevertheless, the KSC remains deeply unpopular in Kosovo. Out of 15 people indicted so far by the KSC, three are serving sentences.

"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February as the proceedings concluded.
Thaci faces a second trial over alleged obstruction of justice, which could mean he will remain in custody even if acquitted on Wednesday in the war crimes case.

articles.title: Who is RJ Nieto, the ex-Duterte blogger appointed as an official under Marcos' admin?
articles.summary: Rey Joseph "RJ" Nieto, better known as the man behind the famous pro-Duterte blog “Thinking Pinoy”, has been appointed as an Assistant Secretary under the Office of the Cabinet Secretary -- the…

blocks.text: Rey Joseph "RJ" Nieto, better known as the man behind the famous pro-Duterte blog “Thinking Pinoy”, has been appointed as an Assistant Secretary under the Office of the Cabinet Secretary — the agency that directly supports President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s office.
But who is Nieto? And how did he cross from one of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s most vocal defenders to an official in the Marcos administration?

During Duterte’s term, Nieto through his political blog site, Thinking Pinoy, had butted heads with several personalities, including former senator Antonio Trillanes III and Pinoy Ako Blogger Jover Laurio.
Oftentimes, Nieto did not merely defend Duterte, but actively launched verbal attacks against the former president’s critics.
In 2017, Trillanes filed a libel case against Nieto after the former made a Facebook post saying that US President Donald Trump called the former senator a “narco”. Nieto pleaded not guilty.
While a Pasay Court junked Trillanes’ case, this is not the only time that Nieto ran into legal trouble due to his blogging.

Nieto, in 2017, had publicly revealed the private information of Laurio, who was then writing the Pinoy Ako Blog anonymously. The Pinoy Ako Blog had criticized alleged misinformation and disinformation during Duterte’s time.
In return, Laurio filed a data privacy complaint against Nieto. In 2023, a Makati court would rule in her favor, finding Nieto guilty and ordering him to pay P350,0000 in damages and legal fees.
On Nieto’s attacks against photojournalist Jes Aznar, the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) said there was no place in the government or the media for “barefaced liars.”

Despite these cases, Nieto would go on several media stints, including making appearances on the People’s Television Network and SMNI. He also served as a social media consultant for the Department of Foreign Affairs in 2017.
Nieto also has a column in the Manila Bulletin, which was still published in September 2026.

In a column Manila Bulletin posted on August 21, 2021 called “I'm going back to school”, Nieto said that after being acquitted from the case that Trillanes filed against him, he began to think if he did the right thing.

He then expressed that his stint as an angry blogger was over. Since he dropped out of the University of the Philippines, Nieto said he was going back to a different school to get a degree in data analytics, and he wanted a Ph.D. in Data Science.
Nieto posted his new appointment on his own Facebook page. He also said that the position is likely not in communications anymore.

“I spent the past years studying mathematics in the University of Bristol. That training taught me to look carefully at evidence, systems and complex problems. Sana magamit ko iyon sa trabaho,” Nieto said.
He said that he is also doing a part-time Master of Science in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Public Policy at the University College London.
In the same Facebook post, Nieto said that he has calmed down after years of shouting online.

“To be frank, haggard ang sigawan. For better or worse, my years away changed me in many ways. Mas kalmado na ako ngayon at mas marunong nang pumili kung alin ang dapat patulan. At least, I would like to think so. Baliw pa rin ako as usual, but mas kalmado na,” Nieto said.

(To be frank, it is tiring to keep shouting. For better or worse, my years away changed me in many ways. I am calmer now and I know when I should fight back. At least, I would like to think so. I am still crazy, as usual, but calm now.)
Marcos sees no colors
In the time since Nieto had stepped back from a pro-Duterte blogger, there was a major falling out between Marcos and Vice President Sara Duterte.
From Uniteam partners, Sara Duterte is now calling for Marcos’ resignation.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro however, said that Marcos does not see colors.

“Kung kayo po ay makikitang magiging asset sa gobyerno para mas maging maganda ang serbisyo ng isang ahensiya, hindi po mag-aatubili ang Pangulo na kayo ay kunin, provided na ang puso po ninyo, kahit ano'ng inyong kulay, dapat ay sa taumbayan at sa bansa hindi sa isang tao o sa isang dati ninyong tinataguyod,” Castro said in a Press briefing.

(If you are seen as a potential asset to the government for better service in an agency, the President will not hesitate to get you, provided that your heart, no matter what your color, should be for the people and the country, not for one person or your former master.)
Castro has yet to disclose details of Nieto’s role in the office of the Cabinet Secretary. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Von der Leyen sets out challenges and opportunities for EU in ‘state of the Union’ speech – Europe live
articles.summary:
European Commission president sets out opportunities and challenges facing the European Union

Von der Leyen frames it as a choice between “independent Europe that stands up…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 3m agoEU's trade relationship with China 'unsustainable' and need to be rebalanced, von der Leyen says
5m ago'We need to electrify Europe,' von der Leyen says, to cut fossil fuel costs down
10m agovon der Leyen warns against anti-European ultranationalists and Russia who 'despise our values'
12m ago'We are now dealing with an openly hostile world,' EU's von der Leyen warns
14m agoEU 'the strongest' but 'most precarious' it has even been, von der Leyen says
36m agoWatch von der Leyen's SOTU live - video
37m agoMorning opening: The state of the European Union

blocks.text: Von der Leyen then turns to investment and growth, as well as the EU’s next budget.
She talks about the need to simplify and tackle fragmentation on investment to help fund European start ups.

She pays specific tribute to the success of ICEYE, a radar satellite imaging and space-based monitoring company, built by Finland’s Pekka Laurila and Poland’s Rafał Modrzewski after they met through Erasmus student exchange programme 15 years ago.
“Today they are one of the world’s leading space technology companies,” she says. “You are a true European success story.”
EU's trade relationship with China 'unsustainable' and need to be rebalanced, von der Leyen says
Von der Leyen turns specifically to China, warning that the EU’s trade deficit with China is now €1bn a day, and it has “reached its tipping point.”

“Some say the second China shock is looming, but it’s already here. It shows in our communities and factories across our union. It leads to deindustrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable.”
She says the EU “will use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationships.”
She also talks about the need to diversify on critical raw materials.
'We need to electrify Europe,' von der Leyen says, to cut fossil fuel costs down
Von der Leyen also talks about the need to reform Europe’s energy market.
She says “Europe cannot remain an industrial powerhouse if its energy prices are structurally too high.”

She says the bloc successfully pivoted towards homegrown cleaner energies in the aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion on Ukraine, but it still “bitterly felt the cost” of the strait of Hormuz closing later.

“We need to double down on our affordable and home-grown clean energy. Be it renewables or nuclear, be it biomethane or others. Technologically neutral. But these energies must give us independence and drive down energy prices.”
She says “we need to electrify Europe,” and cut the fossil fuel import bill.
She says lots of renewable capacity is waiting to be connected, and the EU needs to speed up grid connections.
She then turns to trade.
Von der Leyen says “kickstarting Europe’s economy is our number one priority,” as Europe needs to tap into its huge market, world class industries and services.
She says its single market remains too fragmented and needs to reform further, with the aim of completing it by the end of next year.

“In today’s economy, speed is of the essence. A permanent permit or a form, a grid connection of financing decision – all of this can determine where an investment is made and where jobs are created. We need to move much faster,” she says.
Von der Leyen also talks about the need to simplify its rules.
von der Leyen warns against anti-European ultranationalists and Russia who 'despise our values'
Von der Leyen frames it as a choice between “independent Europe that stands up for its values in this world,” or “letting divisions and dependencies hold us back.”

“Do we want to rally around our European idea that together we can decide our own destiny? Or do we let our democracies be undermined by the proxies and puppets of authoritarians? Whether it is the ultra nationalist or the anti-European, whether it’s Russian interference or disinformation, the names may be different, but their goal is the same. They despise our values and they want to shatter our European unity. So let’s not only fight back against that, but let’s fight together for our European ideal.”
'We are now dealing with an openly hostile world,' EU's von der Leyen warns
Von der Leyen warns that “we are now dealing with an openly hostile world,” in which “old assumptions and relationships have frayed.”
She talks about “a territorial war of aggression” in Ukraine, “a fight for industrial capacities” and “narratives,” and “the dizzying speech of change and technology” impacting people’s lives.

“We see this in the rise of the extreme and the decline of nuance, even in the way that we relate to each other. These real concerns are being weaponised to drive a wedge between us, sometimes from the outside, but too often from the inside. But our path is clear. Building an independent Europe that has the power to act. Nothing can divert us from this. Because in this world, the fate of Europe must remain in the hands of Europeans.”
EU 'the strongest' but 'most precarious' it has even been, von der Leyen says
Von der Leyen begins her speech.
She quotes Charles Dickens’s description of the days of the French Revolution, “it was the best of times; it was the worst of times.”
“It is also a fair description of the world we live in,” she says, as she adds “the speed of change is incredible.”

“I would say the state of our union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been. These two statements may seem incompatible, but they are both true and they reflect these exceptional times.”
She says Europe “has chosen to forge its own path” as it navigates “the complex age of … great possibilities and … great perils.”
Europe is “breaking free from the toxic dependency on Russian fossil fuels,” better prepared to defend itself than ever before, and standing for its values with Ukraine and Greenland, she says.
“In the cold fragility of today’s world, only Europe can provide true sovereignty for Europeans,” she says.
EP’s Metsola sets out what people expect from Europe:

“Our union has always moved forward because people were willing to take a leap where the moment demanded it and turned uncertainty into possibility. People expect a union that does more to protect them, more to support them, and more to fight their corner. They want answers on security, on competitiveness, on affordable homes, on quality jobs, on climate, on borders. They want us to stand up for a Europe of values …”
She goes on, also pointedly mentioning the need to continue supporting Ukraine.
Opening the session, the European parliament president Roberta Metsola welcomes Canada’s Carney, who gets long and warm applause from EU lawmakers.
“They haven’t heard you giving your speech yet,” laughs Metsola.
We are about to start.

blocks.caption: Prime minister Mark Carney participates in a welcoming ceremony with President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It’s also worth noting that this year’s SOTU will see a special guests in attendance: Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney.

blocks.caption: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and Roberta Metsola, President of the European Parliament. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

blocks.text: He will listen to von der Leyen’s speech as Canada seeks closer ties with the EU – particularly on defence, digital regulation and trade - amid growing tensions with and outright repeated threats from US president Donald Trump.
Carney will also address the European parliament on Thursday.
Watch von der Leyen's SOTU live - video
The speech is expected to start in the next 10-15 minutes, so you can watch as the European Parliament’s Hemicycle in Strasbourg is filling up ahead of the speech.
Here’s our live stream for today:
Morning opening: The state of the European Union

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is about to speak at the European parliament to discuss “the state of the Union” in her annual speech about the EU’s place in the ever more complicated world.

blocks.caption: A light illumination on a wall at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA

blocks.text: Her speech in Strasbourg comes as the list of challenges facing the bloc grows ever longer – not least an increasingly aggressive Russia following incidents involving Denmark, Lithuania, and Poland this week. Security is set to be a key theme.

We are also likely to hear about Europe’s competitiveness and its standing in a global race dominated by superpowers like China and the US, as well as the rise of nationalism and populism across the continent and beyond.

Expect updates on other major priorities, too: digital regulation (with a sharp focus on online safety), migration (following the Ceuta crisis in late July), and climate and energy in the wake of another record-breaking summer.
Plenty to cover. I will bring you all the key lines here.
It’s Wednesday, 16 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Limit AI now or humanity will lose its agency, says Nobel laureate Maria Ressa
articles.summary: Nobel laureate Maria Ressa warns that unregulated AI threatens human agency, urging citizens to demand legislation for public safety and accountability from tech companies

blocks.text: MARIA RESSA. Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa of the Philippines poses for a picture outside the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo, Norway, September 4, 2026
Gwladys Fouche/Reuters
Nobel laureate Maria Ressa warns that unregulated AI threatens human agency, urging citizens to demand legislation for public safety and accountability from tech companies

items: Nobel laureate Maria Ressa warns that artificial intelligence is manipulating human needs and could undermine personal agency unless regulated.
Ressa emphasizes the need for citizens to advocate for AI regulation, highlighting that it is a public safety issue rather than a freedom of speech issue.
She calls for accountability from tech companies for the harm caused by their products and suggests creating communication platforms that prioritize public interest over corporate control.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

OSLO, Norway – Artificial intelligence, having hijacked humanity’s attention through social media and our biology by manipulating our need for intimacy, will take away our agency unless we legislate now to limit it, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa said.

The Filipino and American journalist, who jointly won the 2021 award in part for her work documenting the power of large tech companies, serves as co-chair of the United Nations’ international scientific panel on artificial intelligence, tasked with assessing how AI is transforming lives worldwide.
Ressa says citizens must campaign for regulation on AI to put pressure on politicians to introduce legislation.
“It is not a freedom of speech issue to ask for regulation. It’s a public safety issue,” said the co-founder and CEO of news outlet Rappler, a Reuters client.

“I think we’re at that phase where if this doesn’t happen, we will tip … (It) will be beyond our control if we don’t step in now,” she said in an interview during a visit to Oslo to speak at a conference on threats against democracies.

blocks.caption: Anthropic CEO urges AI companies to slow model development amid fears over misuse

blocks.text: “Artificial intelligence is neither artificial nor intelligent. It’s been around for about 70 years, and there have been three waves that have already hit the public,” she said.
She described the first phase as social media platforms capturing attention, polarizing societies and isolating individuals in the process.

“The second phase was hacking our biology, again through intimacy: the chatbots,” Ressa said. “And then the last one is agency itself, through agentic and multi-agentic AI, the frontier models that are creating these machines that don’t just pretend to be human, but act for us.”
Some critics, including U.S. President Donald Trump, have rejected industry calls to regulate AI over fears of losing the AI race to China. Ressa dismissed that argument as “good spin”.

“China actually puts more safeguards in place for its citizens than Silicon Valley does for the rest of the world. If you’re on TikTok, the version of TikTok that is in China has age restrictions,” she said.

Speaking before Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to slow the rate at which they advance model capabilities amid mounting fears of misuse of artificial intelligence, Ressa said the first step to bring about change is to make tech companies accountable.

“The very first one (step) is to actually make the companies responsible for the damage they’ve done,” she said, welcoming the US lawsuits that led Meta Platforms to pay up to $18 billion over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram.

She welcomed moves by the European Union and countries, led by Australia, to put age limits on social media but said it does not tackle the “fundamental flaw” that the tools developed by tech companies are addictive for adults too.

“We know this is harmful, so you should remove the addictive features, not just for teenagers, but for all of us,” Ressa said. “It isn’t just the youth that’s being manipulated politically in every country around the world.”

Communication platforms built by public interest groups, away from the control of Big Tech, should be created, in the same way public works such green parks were created, something Rappler did when it launched Rappler Communities in 2023, she said.

A mobile app built on an open-source, secure and decentralised protocol called Matrix, Rappler Communities allowed the Rappler newsroom to connect with its readers, and the readers among themselves, to “have real conversations”, Ressa said.
Rappler invited other Filipino media to join and is now extending the model to other outlets in Southeast Asia.

“It’s a place where people can be safe in the digital sphere, where they can talk to each other and more importantly, listen to each other so that the great work of democracy happens,” she said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Amici curiae: Should absent senators be allowed to vote?
articles.summary: Former Supreme Court (SC) justices on Wednesday gave their expert opinions on whether senator-judges who have not been present during Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial should be allowed…

blocks.text: Former Supreme Court (SC) justices on Wednesday gave their expert opinions on whether senator-judges who have not been present during Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial should be allowed to vote.

Former chief justices Reynato Puno, Hilario Davide Jr., Artemio Panganiban, and former Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna were invited as amici curiae or friends of the court to provide their opinion on the vote threshold needed to convict an impeached official.
Except for Davide who gave his written position to the Senate impeachment court, Puno, Panganiban and Azcuna personally delivered their opinion before the court.
The 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate."

Davide: “Nevertheless, in light of the disquisitions above on the first issue, we now can conclude that those who are detained, abroad, suspended or whose whereabouts are unknown cannot be included, or must be excluded, from the phrase ‘all the Members of the Senate.’”

According to Davide, the framers of the Constitution could never have intended to include in “all members” senators who have resigned or were expelled, those who suffer from mental infirmity, those suffering from physical incapacity or those in hospitals, those who cannot participate in the hearings and deliberations, those who by reason of some legal impediment or restraints cannot exercise or perform their rights and privileges as an official.

Davide said the last group include those who are charged with plunder and for violation of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practice Act as well as those who have been convicted and are serving their sentence.
Panganiban, meanwhile, questioned whether it was truthful or fair to allow senator-judges to cast their vote despite being absent from the proceedings.

Panganiban: “Should the senators be allowed to vote though they were there in hiding, abroad, legally detained, sick, hospitalized, or otherwise absent, and have not been able to access and examine the documents, have not heard the testimonies, and have not observed the demeanor of the witnesses? To put it more picturesquely, Your Honor, is it truthful and fair? To the parties, to our country, and to our people, to allow those abroad, those looking at the pyramids along the Nile or shopping in the fashion houses of Paris, or riding the romantic gondolas of Venice, or deliberately hiding in the dark corners of the world, while everyone here, everyone here in this hall, is sweating it out, listening to sometimes irrelevant and loquacious lawyers or to humble an ancient amicus curiae like me.”
He said that meaningful adjudication requires active participation in the search for truth and fairness.
For his part, Puno believes that a judge does not need to personally see the demeanor of a witness, although he added that it would be ideal.

Puno: “Thus, an RTC judge who succeeds another RTC judge can decide the cases left by the latter, even if the succeeding judge did not personally hear some of the witnesses who have previously testified. The succeeding judge can rely on the testimony of witnesses as reflected in the transcripts of stenographic notes.”
Meanwhile, Azcuna said that senator-judges who have missed hearings should be allowed to vote as long as they believe that they can render impartial judgement.

Azcuna: “If he or she feels that he or she can render impartial judgment, honestly, according to the Constitution and the laws, then even if he missed one or two, or maybe even substantially, most of the hearings were still...Based on the record, he or she feels that she can honestly judge the respondent, I would allow.”
Senator Rodante Marcoleta is detained over a P75-million plunder case while Senator Jinggoy Estrada is detained over a P573-million plunder charge and a graft charge.

Meanwhile, Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa has not appeared in public since his departure from the Senate premises on May 14, after authorities attempted to serve an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant against him.
In early September, Marcoleta insisted that he still has a voting capacity as a senator-judge. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa
articles.summary:
String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s…

blocks.text: The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.

When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.

Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.

On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.
“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.

blocks.caption: Elizabeth Moselakgomo was abducted and killed while out for a run on 9 September.

blocks.text: South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.

For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.
However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.

The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”

South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.
“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.

Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”
Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.
Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.
Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A protest against femicide in Johannesburg last November. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates for women in the world. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.

“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”
The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.
Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.
“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.
“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”
Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.

She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

articles.title: What amici curiae said about the two-thirds vote to convict an impeachable offiicial
