articles.title: Race for BARMM’s top post could turn into Marcos-Duterte proxy war
articles.summary: The scramble for 41 votes in the BARMM parliament tests whether the Macacua and Murad groups can reconcile or whether the struggle could eventually become a potential arena for a Marcos-Duterte…

blocks.text: The scramble for 41 votes in the BARMM parliament tests whether the Macacua and Murad groups can reconcile or whether the struggle could eventually become a potential arena for a Marcos-Duterte showdown

items: The race for the Bangsamoro region’s first chief minister hangs in the balance, with no single party able to govern alone.

The rivalry between the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) reflects deeper divisions within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), with former leaders now on opposing sides after a leadership change in 2025.

The outcome of the negotiations for control of the regional government could have significant implications for the 2028 presidential elections in the Philippines, as national political forces may become involved in the local power struggle.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The election is over, but the real fight for power in the Bangsamoro region may just be beginning.

The contest for the region’s first elected chief minister is likely to unfold over the next few weeks as rival political camps try to assemble the 41 votes needed to control the new parliament. And what began as a bitter split within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) could now become entangled with the much larger political struggle between President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Vice President Sara Duterte in the context of the 2028 presidential elections.

It could become, in effect, a proxy war played out in the Muslim-majority region between two national political forces, with the shape of the region’s first elected government at stake before the new parliament takes office next month.

blocks.caption: No single party gets majority of first-ever elected Bangsamoro Parliament

blocks.text: The September 14 elections produced a regional parliament in which neither of the two dominant parties can govern alone. The five-month-old Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), led by Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua, won 16 of the 40 regional party seats. The MILF’s United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), led by MILF chairman and former BARMM interim chief minister Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim, won 15.

The BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC), the party established by the region’s long-entrenched political families, ranked third. But the numbers have transformed the BGC and other smaller regional parties from supporting players into potential kingmakers.

Together, the BFP and UBJP have 61 (party and parliamentary districts) of the 80 seats; the remainder would be filled by the other parties and sectoral representatives. If the BFP and UBJP put aside their differences (which doesn’t seem likely at the moment) and form a coalition, then the “boxing bout is over” this early.

In that scenario, the MILF could emerge as the biggest beneficiary of an election that appeared to pit one faction against another. Both parties are led by former MILF figures who fought in the struggle that led to the creation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Macacua and Murad may now lead rival camps, but at their core, both are products of the MILF’s decades-old struggle.

Therefore, a reconciliation would mean that, beneath the rivalry and political realignment, the movement that fought for the Bangsamoro could retain decisive influence over its first elected government. If that happens, then the MILF, in the end, is the big winner.

Macacua and Murad are rivals because of a rupture within the MILF. In March 2025, Marcos replaced Murad as interim chief minister with Macacua, then the MILF’s armed group chief. The leadership change deepened tensions, and several formerly high-ranking MILF figures subsequently jumped from the UBJP to the BFP.

Macacua eventually left the UBJP, first becoming an independent candidate before taking over as BFP leader a month before the election. The MILF central committee later stripped him and several allies of their positions in the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces.
Now, he and Murad will sit in the same elected parliament. They can carry on their feud. Or they can find a way to govern together.
But if they do not, the BGC’s and other group’s seats could become decisive.

There are already signs that BGC may be leaning toward Macacua. But that is not a settled outcome. Knowing how Philippine politics work, a move toward UBJP cannot be ruled out. If BGC joins Murad’s camp, the UBJP would have a potential route to the majority with support from other lawmakers.
BARMM has just entered the period of gapangan, the mad scramble for political support.
The election has supplied the numbers. Now comes the bargaining, and that could acquire a national dimension.

Macacua is closely associated with the Marcos administration — it was the President who turned Murad’s former senior minister and MILF armed wing top commander into BARMM interim chief minister. In 2022, Macacua is said to have supported the presidential bid of Marcos, while the MILF leadership openly backed then-vice president Leni Robredo.

Although he lost the top BARMM post to Macacua via presidential appointment, Murad has remained aschairman of the MILF and the leading figure of the UBJP. If the two camps clash over the chief minister’s post, the Marcos and Duterte forces could see the coalition negotiations as another arena in which influence can be gained or lost. Whoever controls the regional government would be in a strategic position to influence the outcome of the 2028 presidential elections in the BARMM.
The Duterte camp, in particular, could have an incentive to work against Macacua in the election because of his ties to Marcos.

That does not mean that every politician who opposes the BFP is a Duterte ally. Bangsamoro politics has its own alliances, political families, and local calculations that do not always follow the divisions in Manila — or Davao.
But if BFP and UBJP remain locked in their fight, the national divide could become harder to keep outside the room of the BARMM.

A BFP-UBJP reconciliation could keep the center of gravity within the Bangsamoro, bringing two rival MILF factions into one governing arrangement. But a prolonged fight could do the opposite, pulling BGC and the other smaller blocs deeper into the contest and giving national political forces more reason to take an interest.

In the next few weeks, the question will be who can get at least 41 votes, who is willing to make the necessary bargains and whether the struggle remains a Bangsamoro dispute or becomes an arena for a Marcos-Duterte showdown.

The first elected BARMM government of the Bangsamoro will take office next month. Before then, its government may be decided in the backroom negotiations now beginning. Or, it may have already been decided. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Anywhere, anytime’: Victoria police and PSOs to get random stop and search powers after Labor backflip
articles.summary: Premier Ben Carroll adopts Coalition’s stance on Jack’s Law, which gives police and PSOs power to randomly search people for knives with metal detectors The Victorian premier has made another policy…

blocks.text: The Victorian premier has made another policy backflip, announcing a re-elected Labor government would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors – despite experts warning of a lack of evidence that the measure reduces violent crime.

Ben Carroll on Wednesday announced he would match a commitment made by the Coalition opposition last year to introduce Queensland’s Jack’s Law, named after 17-year-old Jack Beasley, who was fatally stabbed in Surfers Paradise in 2019.

Under Labor’s commitment, police and PSOs would receive 1,200 extra handheld metal-detecting wands to use on any person in a public place from early next year. Or as the police minister, Paul Edbrooke, put it: “Anywhere, anytime.”
The bipartisan support for the new powers comes despite warnings from criminologists and human rights advocates that the laws will be ineffective at reducing violence.

Sarah Schwartz, the legal director of the Human Rights Law Centre accused Carroll of “ignoring the evidence and caving into pressure in a race to the bottom to suppress democratic freedoms and human rights”.

“We know from other states that these powers only serve to give police unchecked powers to harass and target people, particularly marginalised groups, while doing nothing to actually keep communities safe,” she said.

A Griffith University study of a 12-month trial of Jack’s Law on the Gold Coast between 2021–22 found there was no reduction in violence as a result of the searches and that they put human rights at risk.

“There’s no evidence that it’s in any way effective in actually reducing knife related violence, which is the whole premise of the law,” Griffith University’s Janet Ransley told the Guardian last year.
Swinburne University criminologist Joel McGregor said “tough-on -crime policies” would do little to address the causes of crime, particularly among young people.

“Police might find a knife or a weapon and they remove that weapon from the street. That’s a great outcome, but it doesn’t address the underlying behaviours as to why that person is carrying the knife or the weapon in the first place,” he said.

Currently in Victoria, police are only authorised to perform warranties pat-down searches in “designated areas.” A six-month designation of the CBD as one was earlier this year deemed invalid by the federal court.
Carroll said the government would work with legal experts to ensure Jack’s Law would be “watertight”.
“Victorians are sick of knife crime, and so am I,” he told reporters.

Jack’s Law has also been replicated in Tasmania, Western Australia and the Northern Territory following advocacy by Jack’s parents. In New South Wales, the warrantless search powers apply only in declared designated areas.
Victorian Labor’s move marks a significant shift for the state government after it had resisted expanding search powers under former leader Jacinta Allan.
After meeting with Beasley’s parents in September 2025, the then-police minister Anthony Carbines said the state’s search powers were sufficient.
after newsletter promotion
“It might not be called Jack’s Law, but what we have in place in Victoria is a safe and effective mechanism that Victoria police asked for,” he said at the time.
Asked repeatedly why there had been a policy change, Carroll answered “I’m the new premier”.
The Victorian Greens’ justice spokesperson Katherine Copsey said the about face showed Labor had “completely lost its way on community safety” and was “just copying whatever the Liberals announce.”

According to Queensland police statistics, police stopped and scanned 160,997 people between 18 July 2025 and 30 June 2026. More than 77% of them were male, and 22.6% of people with a known ethnic origin were Indigenous, despite Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people making up only 4.6% of Queensland’s population.
In Victoria, two years of data obtained by Liberty Victoria revealed just over 1% of the searches conducted in designated areas found illicit items, including weapons.
But Carroll’s shift was welcomed by Jack’s father, Brett Beasley, who said it was “about bloody time”.
“I’ve been pushing for Jack’s Law to be introduced down there for some time now, so it’s great news,” he told ABC Radio Melbourne.
“Put the politics aside and let’s focus on the community safety and that’s what Jack’s Law is all about.”
Additional reporting by Andrew Messenger

articles.title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds
articles.summary: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in…

blocks.text: The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.

Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.

The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.

blocks.caption: Wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank of England’s initial capital, according to Dr Michael Bennett.  Photograph: Alexander Spatari/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.

“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.
“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”

An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge, the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.

The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind the Legacies of British Slavery (LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.

blocks.caption: The Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery.  Photograph: pawopa3336/Getty Images/iStockphoto

blocks.text: The Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.
Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England had owned 599 enslaved people on two plantations.

An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.
The Bank also acknowledged and apologised for past governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.
Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29, was also an MP and defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.

Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an article published on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”

While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.
Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is building from Caribbean and African countries.
A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

articles.title: Fresh evidence of C of E’s role in enslavement uncovered as church wrestles with reparations debate
articles.summary: Register of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyages Nearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian…
articles.byline: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent. Photography by Wayne Crichlow

blocks.text: Nearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian case for reparative justice, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, visited the Ghanaian shore where he was enslaved as a boy.

After witnessing the dungeons beneath the chapel at Cape Coast Castle, once run by the Royal African Company (RAC), Mullally recommitted the Church of England to its “journey of repentance” for its role in slavery.

Back in Britain, historians working on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders were uncovering evidence that C of E clergy financed the RAC, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.

The register, which documents investors in Britain’s nearly 250-year transatlantic slave trade, includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments helped fund hundreds of slaving voyages and a 1720 relaunch of the RAC. Among them was Henry Brydges, later a canon at St Paul’s Cathedral, who bought half of his £10,000 shareholding on the day he became the Archdeacon of Rochester.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register showed a “truly national picture”. Profits from enslavement filtered down to communities “from Cumbria to the Cotswolds” through bequests to parishes – evidence of a history of the C of E “giving slavery its blessing” and raising fresh questions about whether the church is doing enough to atone.

In 2023, church commissioners – the C of E’s asset managers – launched Project Spire, a £100m impact investment fund for communities affected by slavery’s legacies, which has caused division within the church. It is not a reparations fund, but is central to the church’s determination to be a force for justice and healing in the world. It was launched nearly 20 years after Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, rejected the idea that today’s church bears no responsibility for the past.

blocks.caption: The register includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments co-funded hundreds of slaving voyages. Among them was Henry Brydges, later canon of St Paul’s Cathedral, pictured.

blocks.text: However, Spire mainly responds to historic investments in the South Sea Company, which trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved Africans. That represents a “sliver of church complicity”, said Prof Alan Lester, a historical geographer at the University of Sussex.

That complicity helped shape modern Britain, Lester said. Plantation profits helped fuel the Industrial Revolution, railways, public health, welfare, universities, schools, church building and the public finances. “Look at Anglican parishes in Jamaica, their ability to withstand climate change, and compare that with the wealth generated in Britain by the plantation complex,” he said.
For the Rev Natasha Beckles, the dean of racial justice for Willesden, reckoning with this past goes to the heart of Christian faith.
“What was the purpose of the cross if we’re not able to talk about this?” she said. “Slavery made the image of God transactional. There has to be an understanding of the impact on the world.”

blocks.caption: ‘The public and people within the church don’t even know what the extent of the church’s involvement was,’ Dr Leona Vaughn says.

blocks.text: Dr Leona Vaughn of the University of Liverpool, a co-organiser of a 2025 Anglican “truth-telling” event, said: “The public and people within the church don’t even know the extent of the church’s involvement.

“We’ve not even started to come to terms with the ‘Slave Bible’,” she said, a C of E-sanctioned, heavily edited Bible, stripped of liberation narratives, that planters used as a tool of social control from 1807.

The history of the United Society Partners in the Gospel (USPG), the C of E’s 325-year-old missionary partner, shows how powerful Anglicans practised and perpetuated transatlantic chattel slavery – a uniquely racialised, violent system of human commodification and forced mass migration. Today, members of USPG – of which Mullally is president – have committed to “the gospel’s call to break every chain of injustice”.

USPG’s forerunner, the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG), supplied chaplains to the RAC at Cape Coast Castle. For more than 120 years, with the involvement of C of E leaders, SPG enslaved people on the Codrington estate in Barbados, which generated the equivalent of £5m a year in today’s money.

At Codrington, enslaved Africans were branded with the word “Society”, tortured with the lash, straitjacket and iron collar, and worked to death. In seven months in 1746, 19 enslaved people died – including Daniel, who was “shot by accident” – with three deaths in a single day.
Pettigrew said the “clear signal” sent by the C of E’s relationship with Codrington was “if the church is doing it, why shouldn’t I?”
After abolition, SPG and at least 96 clergy who enslaved people received millions in compensation for “loss of property”. In 2023, USPG launched its own £7m reparative justice programme.

Christian collusion can be traced back to a 1452 papal bull authorising the enslavement of non-Christians, the author Malik Al Nasir said. He wants the C of E to digitise its records in the UK and the Caribbean.
after newsletter promotion

In the 17th century, John Cotton, a former Lincolnshire vicar, co-drafted a charter legalising slavery in New England. By the 1750s, high churchmen were codifying pro-slavery ideology: Thomas Newton, later the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, argued Africans were destined to be “servants of servants”, while Thomas Francklin, later the chaplain to George III, said: “We use [African] bodies for our support and happiness.”

blocks.caption: The London skyline from St Paul’s Cathedral, with the City in the distance. Experts say the C of E’s complicity in enslavement helped shape modern Britain.

blocks.text: Some Anglican voices did oppose slavery. Condemning it in 1685, the preacher Morgan Godwyn said: “We have … conspired with Satan.”

Project Spire’s critics have instead focused on the legacy of Anglican abolitionist MPs, such as William Wilberforce. Wilberforce’s 1823 anti-slavery petition was followed by his colleague Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton acknowledging that “we owe a large and liberal atonement”.

In his 1787 book, Cugoano – who won his freedom in England – wrote that the injustice done to Africans “cries aloud for universal reformation and national repentance”. He drew on biblical scriptures such as Numbers, Leviticus, Exodus and Deuteronomy that included reparative principles.

Class shaped church complicity, Beckles said. “The oldest child got the land, the second child they put in the church, the third was sent to the Caribbean.” That meant, Al Nasir said, that “one sibling could profit from slavery while another absolved it – the right hand washing the left”.
Enslaved African Christian leaders helped force the issue of abolition – including Samuel Sharpe, the deacon executed for leading Jamaica’s 1831-32 Baptist war.

The posthumously published Demerara diaries of the English Methodist the Rev John Smith also educated the British public about the relentless beatings, toil and meagre diet – raw yellow plantains – endured by enslaved Africans. Smith’s preaching was blamed by Anglican planters for Guyana’s 1823 Demerara rebellion. He died awaiting execution.

blocks.caption: Thomas Newton, who became the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, said in the 18th century that Africans were destined to be ‘servants of servants’.

blocks.text: The moral conviction of English non-conformists – such as Smith and Quaker abolitionists – contrasts with the 45 C of E clergymen in the register.

The C of E already has an impact investment fund, so insiders have expressed surprise at the backlash against Spire, which is facing a legal challenge. In the House of Commons in September, the MP Marsha de Cordova, the second church estates commissioner, rebutted claims from rightwing critics that Spire diverts money from English churches.

She said the church regarded historic links to slavery with profound regret, that Spire is funded from the commissioners’ own income rather than parish collections, and that the English ministry would receive £1.6bn over three years.

A 2023 report estimated Britain’s slavery debt at £18.6tn. For Beckles, no sum could be enough. “What do you say to a mother who has had her child taken from her? To talk about a figure is grotesque,” she said. “For that level of human suffering, you’d be writing a blank cheque.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

articles.title: People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder
articles.summary: Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last…

blocks.text: Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.

Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.
This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.

Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.

blocks.caption: Asháninka territory in Brazil sits along the winding Amônia River. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community. Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/AP

blocks.text: Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.

On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.
Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.

Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.

Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.

The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.

Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”

At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.

Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.

In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.

blocks.caption: An Indigenous person looks out over Apurímac River valley in Peru. Local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists have been threatened after calling for a more effective state presence across affected countries. Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.

Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.

Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.
Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.

Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”

articles.title: 3 ex-SC justices tell impeachment court: Conviction threshold not fixed at 16
articles.summary: A lower threshold for the number of senators the prosecution must persuade would increase the chances of Sara Duterte being removed from office

blocks.text: IMPEACHMENT COURT. Senators take their oath as they convene as an impeachment court for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, on May 18, 2026.
A lower threshold for the number of senators the prosecution must persuade would increase the chances of Sara Duterte being removed from office

items: Three retired Supreme Court justices argue that the conviction threshold for impeachment is not fixed at 16 votes, suggesting that not all senators should be counted if they cannot participate.
They emphasize that senators who are absent due to legal issues, health problems, or other impediments should be excluded from the vote count.
Only one retired justice supports maintaining the 16-vote threshold, while the Senate impeachment court's presiding officer's ruling on this matter is still pending.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Out of the four retired Supreme Court justices invited by the impeachment court to advise it on the conviction threshold debate, three of them took the position that the number of votes needed to remove the impeached official is not fixed at 16.

Former chief justices Reynato Puno, Hilario Davide Jr., and Artemio Panganiban said on Wednesday, September 16, the constitutional provision stating that no person shall be convicted without a two-thirds vote of all members of the Senate does not automatically put the denominator at 24.

“The framers of the Constitution of 1935, 1973, and 1986 would never have intended to include in ‘all members’… those who cannot participate in the hearings and deliberations on the impeachment, such as those outside the jurisdiction of the Philippines, or whose whereabouts are unknown or are in hiding to avoid arrest,” Davide said in a written position read by the Senate secretary.
He added that those who cannot exercise their rights and privileges as a senator due to “some legal impediment or restraints” such as plunder charge should be excluded from the count.

blocks.caption: 3 ex-SC justices tell impeachment court: Conviction threshold not fixed at 16

blocks.text: Currently, Senator Jinggoy Estrada is suspended from the Senate after his arrest on plunder charges; Senator Rodante Marcoleta is in detention in a separate plunder case; and Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is evading arrest in connection with a crimes-against-humanity case before the International Criminal Court.
In addition, Senator Loren Legarda has been on medical leave for a number of weeks now, preventing her from attending the trial.
Panganiban said the interpretation of charter framers should not necessarily prevail, and must reflect the “common sense of the people,” guided by truth and fairness.

“Is it fair and truthful should the senators be allowed to vote if they were in hiding, abroad, legally detained, sick, hospitalized, or otherwise absent, and have not been able to access the documents, have not heard the testimonies and have not observed the demeanor of the witnesses?” Panganiban asked.
“Is it fair to the parties, to the country, to allow those abroad, looking at the pyramis along the Nile, and shopping at the fashion houses in Paris?” he added.

blocks.caption: 3 ex-SC justices tell impeachment court: Conviction threshold not fixed at 16

blocks.text: Puno argued that if the conviction threshold is fixed at 16, the Constitution should have explicitly said so.
“By using two-thirds, the number of votes to convict will have to move depending on certain factors,” Puno said.

blocks.caption: 3 ex-SC justices tell impeachment court: Conviction threshold not fixed at 16

blocks.text: Only retired Supreme Court justice Adolfo Azcuna took the stand to retain the 16-vote conviction threshold.
“Supermajority threshold is sound constitutional design and should be sustained rather than lowered to a lesser threshold,” Azcuna said.

It remains to be seen whether Senate impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero’s initial ruling to keep the threshold at 16 will be sustained, but the legal luminaries’ position are expected to give a boost of confidence for the prosecution, which had been vocal before the start of the trial about lowering the minimum number of senators needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.
Oral arguments on the subject are scheduled on September 23. – with reports from Sundy Locus/Rappler.com

articles.title: Catapang orders filing of raps vs. ex-CIW officials over alleged misuse of PDL funds
articles.summary: Catapang orders filing of raps vs. ex-CIW officials over alleged misuse of PDL funds

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 12:12pm

Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) Director General Gregorio Catapang Jr. on Wednesday directed the filing of administrative, criminal, and civil complaints against two former superintendents of the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) and five other personnel.
This came following the bureau’s investigation into the alleged missing trust fund of persons deprived of liberty (PDL).

Catapang approved the Directorate for Intelligence and Investigation’s (DII) recommendation to file administrative proceedings before the BuCor Office of Internal Affairs Service against the individuals.
He also directed the filing of criminal and civil cases.

According to BuCor, the former superintendent will face administrative proceedings for gross neglect of duty and grave misconduct for failing to exercise the required diligence in supervising, monitoring, reconciling, and maintaining institutional control over the trust fund.
It also found that she failed to comply with the BuCor PDL Trust Fund Policy.

Aside from this, it found that she authorized the use of the trust fund for the renovation and improvement of the Multipurpose Hall, Overseer’s Office, and Investigation and Verification Section Unit (IVSU).

Meanwhile, the individual who served as acting CIW superintendent was also cited for authorizing the advancement of P300,000 from the fund to cover a remittance for PDLs that reportedly had not been properly transmitted.
According to BuCor, the investigation found that the CIW Trust Fund Officer was unable to account for P5.1 million in PDL Trust Fund.

However, it said that the final audiot report conducted by the BuCor Internal Audit Service reflected an unaccounted amount of P6.4 million without deducting the more than P1.2 million accounted amount yet to be collected or listed as receivables.
Catapang said that a second review will be conducted. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: SC tells Congress: Enact anti-political dynasty law
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, saying its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion, the…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 12:07pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, saying its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion, the High Court's spokesperson, lawyer Camille Ting, said Wednesday.
At a press briefing, Ting said Article II, Section 26 of the 1987 Constitution requires Congress to enact a law prohibiting political dynasties.

“The Court directed Congress to comply with its mandatory constitutional duty to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, define political dynasties, and determine the scope of the prohibition,” she said.
The ruling stemmed from a petition filed in 2025 by several groups and individuals asking the High Court to direct Congress to enact a law against political dynasties.
Section 26 states: “The State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service, and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law.”
Ting said the use of the word “shall” makes clear that the State has a duty to prohibit political dynasties.
“The phrase ‘as may be defined by law’ does not give Congress the choice whether to prohibit political dynasties,” she said.
The SC, however, is leaving it to Congress to define what constitutes a political dynasty and determine the scope of the prohibition.

“The SC found that this interpretation is consistent with the intent of the Constitution’s frameworks. Records of the Constitutional Commission showed that the frameworks agreed to leave the definition of political dynasties to Congress after they could not agree on the specific family relationships… that should be covered,” Ting said.
“Thus, Congress has discretion over how political dynasties should be defined and prohibited, but not whether to enact the law,” she added.
House bill

In June, the House of Representatives passed on third and final reading an anti-political dynasty bill that would ban relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction.

However, business and civic groups have called on the Senate to reject the measure and urged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to veto it, saying it would institutionalize political dynasties rather than dismantle them.
‘Widespread’
According to Ting, the SC took note of the numerous anti-political dynasty bills filed in Congress over the years that remained unacted upon.
The Court also considered studies on the prevalence of political dynasties and their relationship with the country's socioeconomic conditions, she said.
“The SC noted that political dynasties have remained widespread and have extended even to the party-list system,” Ting said.

“Despite changes in the composition of Congress over the years, no comprehensive anti-political dynasty law has been enacted, implying either a lack of interest, avoidance for convenience, or service of self-interest,” she added.
Ting said the SC trusts that Congress will comply with its directive.
She said the Court did not set a specific deadline because the Constitution itself does not provide one.
However, Ting said the absence of a constitutional deadline does not mean Congress may indefinitely postpone its constitutional duty.
Should Congress fail to comply, she advised the public to await further action from the Court.

Meanwhile, Ting said the SC ruled that the Commission on Elections (Comelec) cannot be compelled to issue implementing rules to disqualify candidates who belong to political dynasties or cancel their certificates of candidacy.
“Because there is currently no law defining the prohibition,” she said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Robin Padilla on DOJ subpoena for Bato dela Rosa 'escape:' 'Walang takas na naganap'
articles.summary: Senator Robin Padilla on Wednesday maintained that he did not help his colleague Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa escape amid a warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC).

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 12:03pm
Senator Robin Padilla on Wednesday maintained that he did not help his colleague Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa escape amid a warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Padilla said that he welcomes the subpoena issued to him by the Department of Justice (DOJ) on Tuesday.

"Una, naligayahan po ako. Pagkasabi sa akin ng aking chief legislative officer...Ako po ay naligayahan sapagkat alam naman po natin na itong binabato ito sa atin ay galing sa mga dayuhan, naliligayahan ako kapag galling sa dayuhan kasi parang yung aking pagiging Katipunero ay nabibigyang buhay," he said in a press briefing. "Hindi po ako nalungkot, hindi ako nalugmok."

(First, I was pleased. When my chief legislative officer told me... I was pleased because we know that these allegations being thrown at us come from foreigners. I am happy when it comes from foreigners because it feels like my spirit as a Katipunero is being brought to life. I was not saddened, I was not downhearted.)
The PNP-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) filed a complaint against Padilla and others in May for allegedly helping Dela Rosa escape.

Dela Rosa is the subject of an arrest warrant for “alleged criminal responsibility as an indirect co-perpetrator” in the crimes against humanity of murder from July 3, 2016, until the end of April 2018, where at least 32 persons died.
Authorities tried to serve the warrant on Dela Rosa on May 11, leading to a chase inside the Senate building.
He was later placed under protective custody by the Senate but slipped out of the chamber's premises on May 14. He has not appeared in public since.
Meanwhile, Padilla is facing an obstruction of justice complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman.

"Walang takas na naganap. Napanood ninyo naman yung CCTV. Kayo naman. Mayroon bang ganun tumakas? Siya lang ay sumakay sa aking sasakyan at nakisakay. Hindi naman po magsisinungaling ang CCTV. Panoorin na lang natin yung CCTV kung may naganap na pagtakas," said Padilla.

(No escape occurred. You've watched the CCTV footage anyway. Come on. Is there anyone who escapes like that? He simply got into my vehicle and hitched a ride. The CCTV will not lie. Let's just watch the CCTV to see if an escape actually took place.)
Padilla said that he is ready to appear before the panel of prosecutors and to submit his counter-affidavit on September 25 and October 9.
"Opo, siyempre. Kahit yung advice nila ay 'wag na. Pero siyempre, ayan po ay paggalang sa ating mga namumunong mga opisyal," he said.
(Yes, of course. Even though their advice was not to [appear]. But of course, that is out of respect for our ruling officials.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions
articles.summary:
Study challenges belief that temple’s curves were designed to correct optical illusions that would have ruined its clean lines

A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the…

blocks.text: A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens.

Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon’s clean lines.

But after a detailed investigation, and a flurry of mathematical modelling, Prof Alain Goriely at the University of Oxford has reached an awkward conclusion. The optical illusions the curves are meant to fix are either nonsense or practically imperceptible. In short, the illusions are themselves an illusion.

In his study, Goriely traces the myth back to the 1st-century Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius who wrote about the Parthenon 400 years after its construction. His account found its way into architectural books and became established fact. Today’s AI chatbots still churn out the tale. “I do think it might be the oldest myth that we have,” Goriely said, “apart from religion.”

A common claim that the mathematician challenges concerns the Parthenon’s base or stylobate. Measurements show the sides of the base are not horizontal but form a gentle arc that rises 6cm in the centre. According to Vitruvius, this corrects an illusion that would make the base appear to sag in the middle.
The sagging effect has been attributed to two proposed tricks of the light. The first states that long horizontal lines simply seem to slump in the middle, but Goriely found no evidence for this.

The second suggests that the Parthenon’s marble columns create the illusion. This is based on the Hering illusion where parallel lines on a 2D sheet can look bowed when other lines intersect them. But the Hering illusion is strongest when the intersecting lines are at acute angles. The columns at the Parthenon are too vertical to produce the illusion, and there is no proof it even works in 3D, Goriely said.

Another claim is that the bulges in the Parthenon’s columns – a curvature called entasis – corrects an optical illusion that would make them look too narrow in the middle. Again, Goriely found no evidence for the illusion. Moreover, the columns at the Parthenon bulge by a mere 18mm, which is barely perceptible at typical viewing distances.

Goriely, who assesses and dismisses other supposed “optical corrections” in his paper concedes he “fell into a bit of a rabbit hole” pulling all the evidence together. He suspects the Parthenon’s architects had other reasons for the architectural features.

The curve of the base may have prevented rain puddles forming and curved columns might simply have felt more organic and visually pleasing to the ancient Greeks, he writes in Royal Society Open Science.
It is unclear why the myth has endured for so long, but Goriely suspects that the perception of ancient Greece as a supremely knowledgeable and ingenious civilisation is partly to blame.

Unusually for an academic study, Goriely ends his paper by inviting readers to put it down and take a walk in a city. “Trust your own eyes, question what you see and decide for yourself whether the theory of optical corrections holds up,” he writes.

Frank Salmon, professor of the history of classical architecture at the University of Cambridge, said: “Some experts have long been cautious of Vitruvius’s explanations, recognising the risks inherent in using his text as a sort of bible to explain architectural practices in Greece centuries before his time, but also the loss of the many Greek texts about their temple architecture he claimed to have read when preparing his own.”

articles.title: Students in Gaza ‘devastated’ after plan for them to study in Belgium fails
articles.summary:
Belgian government unable to agree on evacuation of 13 students to take up scholarships at universities

Students who are unable to leave Gaza and take up scholarships at Belgian universities…

blocks.text: Students who are unable to leave Gaza and take up scholarships at Belgian universities have said they are devastated after Belgium’s government hit deadlock on a plan enabling them to leave the war-torn territory.

Ahmed Abujami, a 28-year-old doctor in Gaza, said he was “deeply disappointed” after Belgium’s five-party coalition government last Friday failed to agree on an evacuation plan for 13 students and researchers in the territory. Abujami has a scholarship to do a one-year master’s degree in public health at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. He hopes to gain skills and experience to rebuild Gaza’s shattered health system.

blocks.caption: Ahmed Abujami said he was deeply disappointed by the Belgian government’s failure to agree on an evacuation plan. He hopes to study public health in Antwerp. Photograph: Source- Ahmed Abujami

blocks.text: “I was devastated by the failure to reach an agreement on Friday,” he told the Guardian via a messaging app. “We have already lost so much because of the war and now we are facing the possibility of losing another academic year.”
Like many of the 12 other students, he is unable to apply for a visa to Belgium, which can only be done in person in Jerusalem or Cairo, but is blocked from leaving the Gaza Strip.

He said: “We are 13 students who followed every rule, went through a strict academic selection process and earned scholarships to study in Belgium. We have nothing to do with the political disagreements surrounding our case.”

Salwa Abu Elhaj, a 23-year-old graduate, still hopes to take up her place to study communications sciences at KU Leuven, but said “with every passing day, that hope becomes more difficult. I have worked very hard for this opportunity and it is heartbreaking to see it becoming uncertain because of circumstances that are completely outside my control.”

She lives in central Gaza in a tent with her family, after their home was destroyed and she was forced to move several times. “There is constant uncertainty about safety, food, water, electricity, communication and even what will happen the next day.”

Ahmed Alsalibi, a 39-year-old computer science professor, said the failure of Belgium’s government to reach an agreement had been “painful” for the group. In May 2024, he was awarded a fellowship at the Free University of Brussels (ULB). He hopes to develop artificial intelligence-aided systems that can be used one day in Gaza to help with the efficient dispatch of ambulances and emergency vehicles.
He said his visa has been approved, but he must collect it in person in Cairo, Jordan or Jerusalem. “We hope that the [Belgian] government in the end will decide to help us.”

blocks.caption: Ahmed Alsalibi has a fellowship to study computer science in Brussels, but is unable to leave Gaza. Photograph: Supplied by Ahmed Alsalibi.

blocks.text: The support the students are seeking is not unprecedented. Italy and the UK are among European countries that have negotiated with Israel and neighbouring countries to enable the evacuation of researchers and students in the last year.
The Guardian has seen official letters confirming the scholarships and, in Abujami’s case, emails denying requests for remote application for a visa.

Rectors from seven of the academic institutions involved published a joint article on Monday saying they were outraged by the outcome. “The moral compass of some government partners is missing,” the group wrote in De Standaard.
“These students are not illegal migrants. They were selected for a competitive scholarship by independent selection committees,” they said.
Belgium’s government, an eclectic five-party coalition led by the Flemish nationalist prime minister, Bart De Wever, failed to reach an agreement on a plan to evacuate the 13 students last Friday.

Maxime Prévot, one of Belgium’s deputy leaders and foreign minister, announced he was withdrawing a proposal to evacuate the students. He said it had been “completely rejected” by one coalition partner – understood to be the New Flemish Alliance party – “unless we were prepared to make concessions on returns to Afghanistan and return hubs”.
“Faced with this attempt to hold one issue hostage to another at the expense of people already living in misery I chose to withdraw my proposal. Dignity is not for sale.”

Belgium’s asylum and migration minister, Anneleen Van Bossuyt, opposes entry for the 13 students, without stronger action to ensure people without the right to stay in Belgium leave the country. She wants to see returns to Afghanistan of convicted criminals and other measures to strengthen deportations of irregular migrants.
She has been vocal in her opposition to the students’ entry, arguing it would lead to “a domino effect” if they seek to bring family members or request asylum in Belgium.

Van Bossuyt, a member of the New Flemish Alliance party says the evacuation would set a precedent for other countries. “Why wouldn’t that apply to people from Yemen or Sudan? Or why not Afghan girls who want to study here?,” she told the public broadcaster VRT earlier this month.
Van Bossuyt is expected to make a statement on the issue in the Belgian parliament on Wednesday. Her spokesperson declined to comment ahead of this event.

Writing in De Standaard, the seven rectors say they do not understand the minister’s reasoning, noting the students have scholarships to cover living expenses and are motivated to return home. “The courses they are coming to take align with what Gaza will need for reconstruction. After their studies, they want to return there for that purpose.”
The academic leaders say they continue to press for a solution, adding: “The doors of our lecture halls remain open.”
But with the academic year under way in some universities, the Gaza students are left watching time slip away.
“Our universities are waiting for us, our academic year is already moving forward and every day we remain trapped in Gaza puts our futures at greater risk,” Abujami said.

articles.title: Los Angeles helicopter crash kills at least three people with others injured
articles.summary:
Officials said incident occurred near the site of a deadly bus crash from earlier in the day

A helicopter crash in Los Angeles has killed at least three people, while another person has been…

blocks.text: A helicopter crash in Los Angeles has killed at least three people, while another person has been taken to hospital with their condition unknown, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.
The crash occurred near the site of a deadly bus crash from earlier in the day, officials said.

It was not immediately clear whether some of the people killed in the crash had been on the helicopter. At least one person killed was outside in the parking lot, Capt Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department, said during a news conference.
Silverman described the helicopter as “pretty well destroyed” and said they’re going to have to go through the rubble to see how many victims were on board.
The helicopter crashed into a parking lot, into or next to some parked vehicles, Silverman said.

More than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash, according to the fire department. The fire had damaged four vehicles and two storage containers, but was out by Tuesday evening, according to officials.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will be handling the investigation.

Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Los Angeles, officials said. Photos and videos online showed around half of an SUV lodged into the side of a MTA bus and a large group of fire crew working around the crash.

articles.title: 'Truth, fairness': Ex-CJ Panganiban questions fixed impeachment math
articles.summary: The ex-chief justice raises a point on whether senators who did not hear the case should help decide the verdict.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 11:18am
MANILA, Philippines — Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban said the 16-vote threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte should not be treated as a fixed number.

Appearing before the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16 as an amicus curiae, or friend of the court, Panganiban said the constitutional requirement of "two-thirds of all the members of the Senate" translates to 16 of 24 senators only "in the abstract."
The calculation, he argued, "cannot always be reduced to abstract arithmetic."

Panganiban said senators should approach the constitutional provision with "common sense," guided by "truth and fairness," rather than rely exclusively on either a literal reading of the text or the intent of its framers.
He noted that senator-judges are not sitting as ordinary jurists but as elected representatives exercising the Senate's constitutional power to try impeachment cases.
Should absent senators vote?
Panganiban also questioned whether senators who have not participated in the proceedings should be allowed to cast a vote on Duterte's guilt or innocence.
He said determining the truth in an impeachment trial requires studying evidence and hearing witnesses in person, including observing their body language, tone of voice and spontaneity.
Fairness likewise requires hearing all sides before reaching judgment, he said, quoting the ancient Greek statesman Themistocles: "Strike me as you may, but hear me first."
Panganiban then raised the cases of senators who may be in hiding, abroad, detained, sick, hospitalized or otherwise absent from the proceedings.
Such senators, he said, would not have examined the documents presented to the court, heard the testimony or personally observed the witnesses.
"Meaningful adjudication requires active participation in this search for truth and fairness," Panganiban said.

In one of the sharpest parts of his presentation, he contrasted senators "sweating it out" inside the session hall with absent members who could be sightseeing by the Nile, shopping in Paris, riding gondolas in Venice or "deliberately hiding in the dark corners of the world."
He did not name any senator.

Panganiban's position adds another argument against automatically treating two-thirds of the Senate as a fixed 16 votes, although he did not, in the portions of his presentation summarized Wednesday morning, prescribe a specific alternative number.
Senate has final say
Panganiban also argued that the Senate itself has the final word on an impeachment verdict.
He said the Constitution provides no route for appealing a Senate judgment in an impeachment trial to the Supreme Court.

The high court may intervene only when the Senate commits grave abuse of discretion, he said, such as a capricious, whimsical or arbitrary exercise of judgment amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court cannot step in simply because it disagrees with the wisdom of the Senate's decision, Panganiban added.
The former chief justice is one of four retired Supreme Court justices tapped as amici curiae, or friends of the court, to advise senator-judges on the disputed voting threshold.

Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr., who submitted a written memorandum, separately argued that the two-thirds requirement should be based on senators legally and physically qualified to vote rather than automatically on the full 24-member Senate. — Based on reports from Cristina Chi and Martin Ramos

articles.title: For ex-CJ Davide, 16 votes not necessarily required to convict Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. argued that the two-thirds impeachment threshold should be based only on senators qualified and able to vote.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 10:48am

MANILA, Philippines — Retired chief justice Hilario Davide Jr. argued that the two-thirds threshold in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial should be based only on senators qualified and able to vote, rather than automatically on all 24 Senate seats.
Davide's position was contained in a memorandum submitted as amicus curiae, or friend of the court, which was read before the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16.

He argued that senators facing legal or physical restraints that prevent them from participating in the trial should be excluded from the denominator used to determine the two-thirds vote required for conviction.

Davide, who was a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention and a member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission, said the framers did not specifically debate the meaning of "all the members of the Senate" in the impeachment provision.
But he said they understood "members" to mean senators capable of performing their duties.
Any other interpretation, Davide wrote, would "tolerate an absurdity, and perpetuate an injustice."
Under his interpretation, senators who have resigned or been expelled would not be counted.
He argued that the same should apply to senators unable to participate because of serious physical or mental incapacity, citing examples such as coma or terminal illness.
Davide also said senators who are outside the country, in hiding or whose whereabouts are unknown should be excluded from the count.

He further argued that senators under legal restraint should not form part of the voting body, including those detained while facing plunder or graft charges, those facing other criminal cases under circumstances preventing them from performing their duties, and those convicted and serving sentence.
Davide cited Supreme Court rulings holding that public officials in detention cannot exercise the functions of their office while detained.
'Avelino' case
Davide also addressed the 1949 Supreme Court ruling in *Avelino v. Cuenco*, which has figured in arguments over how the Senate should count its membership.
He said the case was not directly controlling because it dealt with quorum during an ordinary Senate session rather than the constitutionally required vote in an impeachment trial.
Davide nevertheless said the ruling had persuasive value.

In Avelino, two senators were absent, one confined in a hospital and another in the United States. Davide said this effectively left 22 senators capable of acting, making 12 the majority that elected Mariano Cuenco as Senate president.

Applying that reasoning to the impeachment court, Davide argued that senators who are detained, abroad, suspended or otherwise unable to take part in the proceedings should not be counted when determining the voting threshold.
The Senate impeachment court is considering an appeal of presiding officer Chiz Escudero's earlier ruling that 16 votes, or two-thirds of the full 24-member Senate, are required to convict Duterte.
Davide is one of four former Supreme Court justices tapped as amici curiae to advise the impeachment court on the constitutional question.

Retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno and retired Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna were also invited to give their views. Davide submitted a written memorandum instead of appearing personally. — Based on reports from Cristina Chi and Martin Ramos

articles.title: Lost on Mount Fuji off-season? You'll have to pay for your rescue
articles.summary: The fee will be imposed on those who get lost on Japan's most famous mountain during the off-peak seasons.

blocks.text: From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.
The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.
A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.
Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.

"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.
Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.
Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.
They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.
Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.
However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

articles.title: The Palestinian school under siege – podcast
articles.summary: At least five pupils at a village school in the West Bank have been killed in the last year by settlers and soldiers. Emma Graham-Harrison reports on how the school found itself…
articles.byline: Presented by Annie Kelly with Emma Graham-Harrison; produced by Ivor Manley and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli

blocks.text: Waheed Abu Naim is an English teacher at the Al Mughayyir boys’ school in a village in the West Bank. He loves his job, he says. “I am happy to be a teacher. Although we don’t get lots of money, because my students, especially in the morning, wait for me when I enter the school to shake hands, to smile at me while going inside their classes. So it’s a happy life.”

But the last year has been anything but happy for Waheed. His village is now surrounded by settlers, while the military has blocked off every road except one, which has a checkpoint on it. Teachers who live in neighbouring villages cannot always come to work. But worse are the attacks on the village by settlers.
In April, a 14-year-old pupil was killed next to a playground gate after a gunman opened fire. As Waheed rushed the teenager to hospital he learned his own brother had also been killed.

Senior Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison tells Annie Kelly: “We’ve documented the hundreds of children who’ve been killed by Israeli soldiers, settlers over the last three years. But even in that context, of sort-of regular deadly violence, there is something particularly horrific about someone taking aim at a school full of children.”

Four other students were also killed and, says Emma, things don’t seem to be getting better. “In the next few months I’m just, very unfortunately, expecting to see at least the same level of violence and frankly, probably an escalation.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia warns of ‘red line’ after Houthi drone intercepted close to holy city of Mecca
articles.summary:
The Iran-aligned militant group rejected the suggestion it had targeted Mecca, while the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned the attack

Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, according to a ⁠spokesperson for the ⁠Saudi-led ​military coalition which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen.

The security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”, ⁠coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the ⁠Houthis.

Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest ​city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims ‌undertake each year.
Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, after what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017.

A Houthi official rejected the claim on Wednesday, with spokesperson Hazem al-Assad writing on X: “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.”

The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned what they called a “heinous” attack on Islam’s holy city, blaming the Houthis. The group – which is made up of 57 Muslim-majority countries decried the “ongoing aggression against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.”

Saudi Arabia issued security alerts across parts of the country on Tuesday, including in Mecca and other ‌cities, following a week of attacks by Iran-aligned fighters that have drawn the kingdom deeper into the Middle East ​war.

The Houthis have seized control of parts of ⁠Yemen’s Red Sea coast overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, one of the ​world’s most important ​shipping straits, threatening Saudi oil ​exports rerouted from the strait of Hormuz.
The group has ​announced several major ‌attacks on ​Saudi Arabia over ​the past week, including strikes on an airbase on Monday that it said were retaliation for airstrikes on Yemen.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Human remains found in Arizona after deadly Grand Canyon flash floods
articles.summary:
Hiker Timothy Smith, 53, missing after late-August floods but officials decline to identify remains

Human remains have been discovered near Arizona’s Crystal Rapids, over two weeks after a…

blocks.text: Human remains have been discovered near Arizona’s Crystal Rapids, over two weeks after a flash flood tore through the Grand Canyon, leaving two people dead and one person missing.
National Park Service personnel recovered the remains, before transferring them to the Coconino county medical examiner’s office, the agency confirmed over email.

In late August, heavy rains brought a deluge of flood water barreling through the Grand Canyon national park. The bodies of a Texas chiropractor and a martial artist were recovered, according to the Associated Press. One hiker, Timothy Smith, a 53-year-old pilot from Wyoming, is unaccounted for.
The National Park Service did not identify who the remains belonged to, adding that no further information would be available at this time.
A Facebook account appearing to belong to the wife of the missing pilot, Carrie Smith, acknowledged the discovery of human remains.
“We ask that you continue to pray alongside us! Please be considerate of those handling the situation and those going through this difficult time,” Smith wrote in a Tuesday post.
In earlier Facebook posts, Smith described her husband as an outdoors aficionado.
“Tim loves to show us somewhere new and take us back to the places we love,” she wrote. “We know the search teams are working hard to bring Tim home to us.”

articles.title: Russia plotting to kill targets in US and Europe, federal officials say
articles.summary:
Intelligence services allegedly attempted to pay people to surveil and kill people perceived to be aligned with Ukraine

Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted…

blocks.text: Russia’s intelligence services are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the United States and in European nations supporting Ukraine, federal authorities said Tuesday as they announced charges against five people who remain at large.

An indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court said a network of the intelligence services had paid and attempted to pay individuals in the United States and in other countries to surveil targets to be killed with plans to then kill them.

The associates recruited in the network also had been solicited to carry out acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that were perceived to be aligned with Ukraine, the indictment said.

James Barnacle Jr, head of New York’s FBI office, said the FBI disrupted the plans “through relentless work” as members of the Russian intelligence services and their affiliates “conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world”.

Darren Cox, head of the Washington DC office of the FBI, cited “extraordinary work by multiple FBI field offices, components, and partner agencies that collectively disrupted Russia’s attempts to conduct violent acts in our nation’s capital and throughout the United States”.

He said in a release that when the threat was first identified, the FBI’s Washington field office and its partners “moved quickly to disrupt the plot and hold the Russian government accountable for its actions”.

According to the release, a network of people working for the Russian Federation’s intelligence services had since at least 2024 conspired to conduct and had conducted attacks and murders around the world, including within the United States.
It called the Russian intelligence services network “one arm” of the Russian Federation’s apparatus designed to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world.
Previously, the release said, the network had focused on Russian dissidents and defectors but most recently had targeted nations perceived to be allies of Ukraine.
Recently, it said, members of the network had tried to recruit multiple people in the United States.
Authorities said the network this summer recruited an individual based in the United States to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident it believed to be residing in the United States.

The indictment said a person identified only as “US Resident-1” had been sent to two locations associated with the targeted victim and was given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance” while being promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the work.

After conducting the surveillance and providing multiple photographs and videos of locations associated with the intended victim to one of the men charged in the indictment, the US resident turned down the $40,000 that was offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target through murder.

When the offer was rejected, the member of the intelligence services who had made it tried to recruit multiple other people within the United States to do the job by offering them substantial amounts of money, the indictment said.
